1
序
Preface.
2
夫帝王者，配德天地，葉契陰陽，發號施令，動關幽顯，休咎之徵，隨感而作，故《書》曰：「惠迪吉，從逆凶，惟影響。 」昔伏羲氏繼天而王，受《河圖》，則而畫之，八卦是也。 禹治洪水，賜《洛書》，法而陳之，《洪範》是也。 聖人行其道，寶其真，自天祐之，吉無不利。 三五已降，各有司存。 爰及殷之箕子，在父師之位，典斯大範。 周既克殷，以箕子歸，武王虛己而問焉。 箕子對以禹所得《雒書》，授之以垂訓。 然則《河圖》、《雒書》相為經緯，八卦、九章更為表裏。 殷道絕，文王演《周易》； 周道弊，孔子述《春秋》。 奉乾坤之陰陽，郊洪範之休咎，天人之道粲然著矣。
The sovereign aligns his virtue with Heaven and Earth and moves in concert with yin and yang; when he issues orders, his influence reaches every realm, seen and unseen, and portents of weal or woe answer human conduct. Hence the Book of Documents: walk the straight path and you are blessed; walk the crooked path and you meet disaster—as inevitably as shadow follows form and echo follows sound. In high antiquity Fuxi received Heaven's mandate; the River Chart was revealed to him, and from its pattern he drew the Eight Trigrams. When Yu mastered the floods, Heaven granted him the Luo Document; he codified its teaching in the text we call the Hong Fan. When the sage upholds that Way and cherishes its truth, Heaven lends its aid, and every outcome turns fortunate. From the age of the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors onward, each era retained its proper institutions. This tradition reached Jizi under the Yin, who as royal instructor guarded the Great Plan. After the Zhou overthrew Yin, they brought Jizi home from captivity, and King Wu humbled himself to seek his counsel. Jizi replied with the teaching of the Luo Document that Yu had received, transmitting its lessons for posterity. The River Chart and Luo Document interlock like warp and weft; the Eight Trigrams and the nine divisions of the Hong Fan form an outer shell and inner core of meaning. When Yin's mandate failed, King Wen elaborated the Zhou yi; when Zhou rule decayed, Confucius compiled the Spring and Autumn Annals. He honored the cosmic polarity of Qian and Kun and presented at the suburban altar what the Hong Fan teaches about blessing and blame, so that the bond between Heaven and humanity stood forth in plain sight.
3
漢興，承秦滅學之後，文帝時，虙生創紀《大傳》，其言五行庶徵備矣。 後景武之際，董仲舒治《公羊春秋》，始推陰陽，為儒者之宗。 宣元之間，劉向治《谷梁春秋》，數其禍福，傳以《洪範》，與仲舒多所不同。 至向子歆治《左氏傳》，其言《春秋》及五行，又甚乖異。 班固據《大傳》，采仲舒、劉向、劉歆著《五行志》，而傳載眭孟、夏侯勝、京房、谷永、李尋之徒所陳行事，訖于王莽，博通祥變，以傳《春秋》。
After the Han rose from the wreckage of learning under the Qin, Emperor Wen's reign saw Fu Sheng compile the Great Tradition of the Documents, setting out the Five Phases and their prodigies in full. Between Emperors Jing and Wu, Dong Zhongshu worked the Gongyang tradition of the Annals and pioneered yin-yang interpretation, winning recognition as the doyen of Confucian learning. Under Xuandi and Yuandi, Liu Xiang took up the Guliang Annals, correlated fortunes and disasters with the Hong Fan, and often parted company with Dong Zhongshu. Liu Xin's scholarship on the Zuo Commentary produced yet another, sharply divergent reading of the Annals and the Five Phases. Ban Gu built on the Great Tradition and the three masters—Dong Zhongshu and the two Lius—to write the Han Treatise on the Five Phases, weaving in episodes cited by Sui Meng, Xiahou Sheng, Jing Fang, Gu Yong, Li Xun, and others down to Wang Mang, so that strange blessings and calamities illustrated the moral lessons of the Annals.
4
綜而為言，凡有三術。 其一曰，君治以道，臣輔克忠，萬物咸遂其性，則和氣應，休徵效，國以安。 二曰，君違其道，小人在位，眾庶失常，則乖氣應，咎徵效，國以亡。 三曰，人君大臣見災異，退而自省，責躬修德，共禦補過，則消禍而福至。 此其大略也。 輒舉斯例，錯綜時變，婉而成章，有足觀者。 及司馬彪纂光武之後以究漢事，災眚之說不越前規。 今采黃初以降言祥異者，著於此篇。
Taken together, the doctrine falls under three heads. First: when the ruler follows the true Way and his ministers serve with unstinting loyalty, creation thrives, harmonious energies gather, felicitous signs appear, and the realm rests at peace. Second: when the ruler abandons the Way, mean men fill office, and the people fall into disorder, malignant influences answer with ill omens and the state is undone. Third: when ruler and high ministers heed prodigies, look inward, accept blame, reform conduct, and jointly correct faults, calamity yields and fortune follows. Such is the outline of the theory. Applying these patterns across shifting ages yields a coherent narrative well worth study. When Sima Biao continued the Later Han narrative from Guangwu onward, his treatment of disasters stayed within the earlier framework. Here I collect records of omens and prodigies from the Wei founding (Huangchu) forward and present them in this treatise.
5
五行
The Five Elements.
6
《經》曰：「五行：一曰水，二曰火，三曰木，四曰金，五曰土。 水曰潤下，火曰炎上，木曰曲直，金曰從革，土爰稼穡。」
The classic text runs: "The Five Elements: first water, second fire, third wood, fourth metal, fifth earth. Water sinks and nourishes; fire climbs and burns; wood bends and straightens; metal yields to the forge; earth receives sowing and harvest."
7
=
Typographical section divider.
8
木
Wood.
9
=《傳》曰：「田獵不宿，飲食不享，出入不節，奪農時及有奸謀，則木不曲直。」
The commentary reads: "When rulers hunt without restraint, feast without ritual sacrifice, come and go without measure, disrupt the farming calendar, or plot treachery, wood loses its property of bending true."
10
說曰：木，東方也。 于《易》，地上之木為《觀》。 于王事，威儀容貌亦可觀者也。 故行步有佩玉之度，登車有和鸞之節，三驅之制，飲食有享獻之禮； 出入有名，使人以時，務在勸農桑，謀在安百姓，如此，則木得其性矣。 若乃田獵馳騁，不反宮室； 飲食沈湎，不顧法度； 妄興徭役，以奪農時； 作為奸詐，以傷人財，則木失其性矣。 蓋工匠之為輪矢者多傷敗，及木為變怪，是為不曲直。
The gloss runs: wood belongs to the east. In the Zhou yi, wood resting on earth forms the hexagram Guan—Looking Down. In governance, ritual bearing and personal presence are likewise there to be judged. Hence measured pace with jade pendants at the belt, harmonized bells when mounting a chariot, the thrice-driven hunt, and at meals the proper rounds of offering and tasting; comings and goings are regulated, labor is summoned in season, policy promotes tillage and silkworms, and planning aims at the people's welfare—then wood keeps its true nature. But endless hunting and reckless riding that keep the ruler from his halls; gluttony and drunken heedless of law; arbitrary corvée that steals the seasons of plough and weed; and treacherous schemes that strip the people of their substance—then wood forfeits its nature. Wheelwrights and fletchers then find their timber spoiled, and when timber behaves monstrously, that is the fault called failure to bend straight.
11
魏文帝正月，雨，木冰。 案劉歆說，上陽施不下通，下陰施不上達，故雨，而木為之冰，氛氣寒，木不曲直也。 劉向曰，冰者陰之盛，木者少陽，貴臣卿大夫象也。 此人將有害，則陰氣脅木，木先寒，故得雨而冰也。 是年六月，利成郡兵蔡方等殺太守徐質，據郡反。 太守，古之諸侯，貴臣有害之應也。 一說以木冰為木介，介者甲兵之象。 是歲，既討蔡方，又八月天子自將以舟師征吳，戍卒十餘萬，連旌數百里，臨江觀兵，又屬常雨也。
In the first month of Wei Emperor Wen's reign, rain fell and trees glazed with ice. Liu Xin explained it thus: yang above failed to reach downward, yin below failed to rise; rain fell and sheathed the trees in ice—the air had turned bitter—so wood lost its quality of bending true. Liu Xiang said ice marks yin at its height; wood stands for lesser yang and emblems high ministers and grandees. When such a man is marked for harm, yin first grips the wood—the timber turns cold—so rain freezes upon it. That sixth month, troops in Licheng commandery led by Cai Fang murdered Prefect Xu Zhi and rose in revolt, holding the district. The prefect stood where ancient feudal lords once stood; the omen answered injury to a minister of rank. Another reading treats glazed trees as "armored wood," armor being an emblem of arms. The same year saw Cai Fang crushed; then in the eighth month the emperor took the fleet against Wu—well over a hundred thousand men, banners strung for hundreds of li, maneuvers along the Yangzi—and the rains still would not end.
12
元帝二月辛未，雨，木冰。 後二年，周顗等遇害，是陽施不下通也。
On the xinwei day of the second month under Emperor Yuan, rain fell and the trees iced. Two years later Zhou Yi and his fellows perished by violence—yang failing to reach below.
13
穆帝正月乙巳，雨，木冰。 是年殷浩北伐，明年軍敗，十年廢黜。 又曰，荀羨、殷浩北伐，桓溫入關之象也。
On yisi in the first month of Emperor Mu, rain and glazed trees followed. That year Yin Hao marched north; the next year his army was routed and he languished in disgrace for a decade. Some add that it foreshadowed Xun Xian and Yin Hao's northern campaigns and Huan Wen's thrust into the passes.
14
孝武帝十二月乙巳，雨，木冰。 明年二月王恭為北籓，八月庾楷為西籓，九月王國寶為中書令，尋加領軍將軍，十七年殷仲堪為荊州，雖邪正異規，而終同夷滅，是其應也。
On yisi in the twelfth month of Emperor Xiaowu, rain fell and trees iced again. The year after, Wang Gong took the northern frontier in the second month; Yu Kai the western frontier in the eighth; Wang Guobao became Palace Secretariat Director in the ninth and soon added command of the imperial guards; in the seventeenth year Yin Zhongkan took Jingzhou—wickedly inclined or loyal, they were all swept away in the end, matching the sign.
15
吳孫亮，諸葛恪征淮南，後所坐聽事棟中折。 恪妄興征役，奪農時，作邪謀，傷國財力，故木失其性致毀折也。 及旋師而誅滅，于《周易》又為「棟撓之凶」也。
Under Sun Liang of Wu, after Zhuge Ke's Huainan expedition the ridgebeam of his audience hall snapped at mid-span. Ke had launched needless wars and labor levies, stolen the farming seasons, spun wicked plots, and drained the treasury—wood therefore lost its nature and the timber gave way. When the army turned home he was put to death and his line cut off—the Zhou yi calls such a fate "the peril of the sagging ridgepole."
16
武帝五月，宣帝廟地陷，梁折。 八年正月，太廟殿又陷，改作廟，築基及泉。 其年九月，遂更營新廟，遠致名材，雜以銅柱，陳勰為匠，作者六萬人。 至十年四月乃成，十一月庚寅梁又折。 天戒若曰，地陷者分離之象，梁折者木不曲直也。 明年帝崩，而王室遂亂。
In the fifth month of Emperor Wu's reign the earth subsided at Emperor Xuan's temple and a beam cracked. The first month of the eighth year saw the Grand Temple hall sink again; they rebuilt the shrine, driving piles until they struck groundwater. That September they began a new temple complex, hauling in prized timber and setting bronze columns; Chen Xiu directed the work with sixty thousand hands. It stood finished only in the fourth month of the tenth year; that November another beam split on the gengyin day. Heaven seemed to warn: subsiding earth betokens division; a snapped beam means wood no longer runs true. The emperor died the next year, and the house of Jin slid into turmoil.
17
惠帝，成都王穎使陸機率眾向京都，擊長沙王乂，及軍始引而牙竿折，俄而戰敗，機被誅，穎遂奔潰，卒賜死。 此奸謀之罰，木不曲直也。
Under Emperor Hui, Chengdu Prince Sima Ying sent Lu Ji toward the capital against Changsha Prince Sima Yi; the army had scarcely marched when the banner staff snapped; defeat followed quickly—Lu Ji was killed, Ying fled in rout, and was ultimately forced to kill himself. That was Heaven's rebuke for treacherous design—the fault of wood failing to bend straight.
18
元帝，王敦在武昌，鈴下儀仗生華如蓮華，五六日而萎落。 此木失其性。 干寶以為狂華生枯木，又在鈴閣之間，言威儀之富，榮華之盛，皆如狂華之發，不可久也。 其後王敦終以逆命加戮其屍。 一說亦華孽也，于《周易》為「枯楊生華」。
Under Emperor Yuan, while Wang Dun held Wuchang, lotus-like blossoms burst from the halberds of his escort; within five or six days they shriveled away. Wood had lost its proper nature. Gan Bao read it as freak blooms on dead timber inside the bell pavilion: pomp and glory blazing up only to fade, no more durable than those unnatural flowers. Wang Dun later rebelled and, dead, was dishonored on the corpse. Another view calls it a floral anomaly—the Zhou yi speaks of "withered willows sending forth blossoms."
19
桓玄始篡，龍旂竿折。 時玄田獵無度，飲食奢恣，土木妨農，又多奸謀，故木失其性。 天戒若曰，旂所以掛三辰，章著明也，旂竿之折，高明去矣。 玄果敗。
When Huan Xuan began his usurpation, the dragon-banner staff broke. He hunted without restraint, feasted recklessly, poured labor into works that stole farmers from the fields, and spun endless intrigue—wood therefore lost its nature. Heaven's warning: the standard displays the three luminaries and proclaims authority—snap the staff and the high splendor departs. Huan Xuan was indeed destroyed.
20
=
Typographical section divider.
21
火
Fire.
22
=《傳》：「棄法津，逐功臣，殺太子，以妾為妻，則火不炎上。」
The commentary states: "Neglect law and duty, banish those who built your throne, murder the heir, and elevate a concubine to wife—then fire will not rise as it should."
23
說曰：火，南方，揚光輝為明者也。 其于王者，南面向明而治。 《書》云：「知人則哲，能官人。 」故堯舜舉群賢而命之朝，遠四佞而放諸野。 孔子曰：「浸潤之譖，膚受之訴，不行焉，可謂明矣。 」賢佞分別，官人有序，帥由舊章，敬重功勳，殊別嫡庶，如此則火得其性矣。 若乃通道不篤，或耀虛偽，讒夫昌，邪勝正，則火失其性矣。 自上而降，及濫炎妄起，焚宗廟，燒宮館，雖興師眾，不能救也，是為火不炎上。
The gloss: fire is the south, the force that lifts radiance into clear light. The true king faces south into the light and there holds court. The Book of Documents says: "To know your men is wisdom; that wisdom lets you place them in office." Hence Yao and Shun filled court with the worthy and drove the four villains to the wilds." Confucius added: "Where dripping slander and skin-deep accusations gain no foothold, that ruler may be called clear-sighted." Distinguish true men from sycophants, order appointments by merit, hew to established statutes, honor service, and separate heir from concubine-born sons—then fire keeps its nature." Pursue the Way without conviction, parade hollow shows, let slanderers thrive and the crooked prevail—fire then loses its nature. Then flame drops from above—fires rage unchecked, torches the ancestral shrines and halls; no host however large can stop it: that is fire refusing to rise properly.
24
魏明帝五月，清商殿災。 初，帝為平原王，納河南虞氏為妃。 及即位，不以為-{后}-，更立典虞車工卒毛嘉女為-{后}-。 -{后}-本仄微，非所宜升，以妾為妻之罰也。
In the fifth month of Wei Emperor Ming, fire consumed the Qing Shang Hall. Earlier, as Prince of Pingyuan, he had married a daughter of the Yu clan from Henan. At his accession he refused her the empress's seat and raised instead the daughter of Mao Jia, a wheelwright in the palace workshops. Her origins were low—she ought never to have been lifted so high; Heaven punished the offense of making a concubine into a wife.
25
六月，洛陽宮鞠室災。 二年四月，崇華殿災，延于南閣，繕復之。 至三年七月，此殿又災。 帝問高堂隆：「此何咎也？ 于禮寧有祈禳之義乎？ 」對曰：「夫災變之發，皆所以明教誡也，惟率禮修德可以勝之。 《易傳》曰：『上不儉，下不節，孽火燒其室。 』又曰：『君高其臺，天火為災。 』此人君苟飾宮室，不知百姓空竭，故天應之以旱，火從高殿起也。 案《舊占》曰：『災火之發，皆以臺榭宮室為誡。 』今宜罷散作役，務從節約，清掃所災之處，不敢於此有所營造，萐莆嘉禾必生此地，以報陛下虔恭之德。 」帝不從。 遂復崇華殿，改曰九龍。 以郡國前後言龍見者九，故以為名。 多棄法度，疲眾逞欲，以妾為妻之應也。
That sixth month the polo grounds hall in the Luoyang palace burned. The fourth month of the second year brought fire to Chonghua Hall, which spread to the south annex before crews rebuilt it. By the seventh month of the third year the same hall burned again. The emperor asked Gao Tanglong, "What offense does this mark? Does ritual allow us merely to pray it away?" He replied, "Every prodigy is Heaven's lesson; only ritual observance and virtue can master it. The Yi commentary warns: when those above will not stint and those below will not curb appetite, baleful fire consumes the hall. It adds: heap your terraces too high and Heaven's fire answers with disaster. Heaven answers a ruler who decks out his halls while his people are bled dry: drought follows, and flame leaps from the highest roof. The Old Omens record: disaster fire always singles out towers and palace halls as its warning. Cease the labor drafts, practice austerity, cleanse the scorched ground, and build nothing new there—auspicious grain will rise there to answer your sober virtue. The emperor refused. They rebuilt Chonghua Hall and renamed it the Nine Dragons Hall. Nine jurisdictions had reported dragon sightings; that number supplied the new name. It matched repeated disregard of law, grinding the people down for pleasure—the price of elevating a concubine to wife.
26
吳孫亮十二月，武昌端門災，改作，端門又災。 內殿門者，號令所出； 殿者，聽政之所。 是時諸葛恪執政，而矜慢放肆，孫峻總禁旅，而險害終著。 武昌，孫氏尊號所始。 天戒若曰，宜除其貴要之首者，恪果喪眾殄人，峻授政於綝，綝廢亮也。 或曰，孫權毀撤武昌以增太初宮，諸葛恪有遷都意，更起門殿，事非時宜，故見災也。 京房《易傳》曰：「君不思道，厥妖火燒宮。」
In Sun Liang's twelfth month Wuchang's main gate caught fire; after repairs it burned again. The inner hall gate is where edicts are proclaimed; the hall is where affairs of state are conducted. Zhuge Ke governed with swagger and license; Sun Jun led the palace troops—cruel harm showed itself in the end. Wuchang was where the Sun clan first assumed kingship. Heaven seemed to demand the head of the mighty: Ke lost his army and his life, Jun passed power to Sun Lin, and Lin cast Sun Liang down. Others blame Sun Quan's dismantling of Wuchang for Taichu Palace and Zhuge Ke's plan to move the capital and rebuild gates—ill-timed work that drew the portent. Jing Fang's Yi commentary: neglect the Way and the omen is flame consuming the palace.
27
二月朔，建鄴火，人之火也。 是秋，孫綝始執政，矯以亮詔殺呂據、滕胤。 明年，又輒殺硃異。 棄法律逐功臣之罰也。
Jianye burned on the second month's new moon—fire set by human hands. That autumn Sun Lin took power and forged an edict in Sun Liang's name to execute Lu Ju and Teng Yin. The next year he put Zhu Yi to death on his own authority. Heaven's sentence for abandoning statute and banishing loyal servants.
28
孫休二月，城西門北樓災。 六年十月，石頭小城火，燒西南百八十丈。 是時嬖人張布專擅國勢，多行無禮，而韋昭、盛沖終斥不用，兼遣察戰等為內史，驚擾州郡，致使交趾反亂，是其咎也。
Under Sun Xiu, in the second month, the north tower at the west gate burned. In the sixth year's tenth month fire swept the Shitou citadel, scorching a hundred eighty zhang along the southwest wall. Favorite Zhang Bu dominated the court and flouted propriety; Wei Zhao and Sheng Chong remained sidelined; inspection officers installed as interior clerks harassed the provinces until Jiaozhi rose in revolt—that was the guilt.
29
孫皓三月，大火，燒萬餘家，死者七百人。 案《春秋》齊大災，劉向以為桓公好內，聽女口，妻妾數更之罰也。 時皓制令詭暴，蕩棄法度，勞臣名士，誅斥甚眾，後宮萬餘，女謁數行，其中隆寵佩皇后璽綬者又多矣，故有大火。
Sun Hao's third month brought a conflagration—ten thousand homes lost, seven hundred lives. The Spring and Autumn records Qi's great blaze; Liu Xiang blamed Duke Huan's harem intrigues and shifting wives. Hao ruled by cruelty and caprice, cast law aside, purged scholars and officials, kept ten thousand palace women, and let favorites—even some bearing empress regalia—run wild; the inferno answered that.
30
武帝三月乙丑，震災西閣楚王所止坊及臨商觀窗。 十年四月癸丑，崇賢殿災。 十一月庚辰，含章鞠室、修成堂前廡、景坊東屋、暉章殿南閣火。 時有上書曰：「漢王氏五侯，兄弟迭任，今楊氏三公，並在大位，故天變屢見，竊為陛下憂之。 」由是楊珧求退。 是時帝納馮紞之間，廢張華之功，聽楊駿之讒，離衛瓘之寵，此逐功臣之罰也。 明年，宮車宴駕。 其後楚王承竊發之旨，戮害二公，身亦不免。 震災其坊，又天意乎。
Emperor Wu's third month, yichou day: lightning scarred the Prince of Chu's west-pavilion ward and the Linshang Observatory windows. The tenth year's fourth month, guichou day: Chongxian Hall burned. Eleventh month, gengchen day: fire took Hanzhang racquet hall, Xiucheng Hall's front colonnade, Jingfang's east wing, and Huizhang Hall's south arcade. A memorial warned: Han's five Wang marquises rotated power among brothers; now three Yang dukes tower together—Heaven keeps signaling alarm. Yang Yao thereupon sought to withdraw. The emperor heeded Feng Xian's slander, dismissed Zhang Hua's service, swallowed Yang Jun's malice, and cast off Wei Guan—Heaven's rebuke for banishing loyal ministers. The next year the emperor died. Then the Prince of Chu, seizing a secret pretext, slew both dukes and soon perished himself. Lightning had scarred his ward—Heaven speaking again?
31
惠帝閏月庚寅，武庫火。 張華疑有亂，先命固守，然後救火。 是以累代異寶，王莽頭，孔子屐，漢高祖斷白蛇劍及二百八萬器械，一時蕩盡。 是後湣懷太子見殺之罰也。 天戒若曰，夫設險擊柝，所以固其國，儲積戒器，所以戒不虞。 今塚嗣將傾，社稷將泯，禁兵無所復施，皇旅又將誰衛。 帝后不悟，終喪四海，是其應也。 張華、閻纂皆曰，武庫火而氐羌反，太子見廢，則四海可知。」
Emperor Hui, intercalary month, gengyin day: the imperial armory burned. Zhang Hua feared revolt, secured the site first, then fought the flames. Generations of relics vanished at once: Wang Mang's skull, Confucius's sandal, Gaozu's sword from the white-snake omen, and 2.08 million weapons. It foretold the murder of Crown Prince Minhuai. Heaven warned: ramparts and night watches brace the realm; arsenals guard against surprise. The heir teeters, the altars face ruin, palace guards lose purpose—who will shield the throne? Ruler and consort ignored it and lost the empire—that was the fulfillment. Zhang Hua and Yan Zuan said: armory fire with Di and Qiang in revolt and the heir deposed tells you all you need of the realm.
32
八年十一月，高原陵火。 是時賈后凶恣，賈謐擅朝，惡積罪稔，宜見誅絕。 天戒若曰，臣妾之不可者，雖親貴莫比，猶宜忍而誅之，如吾燔高原陵也。 帝既眊弱，而張華又不納裴頠、劉卞之謀，故後遂與謐殺太子也。 干寶以為「高原陵火，太子廢之應。 漢武帝世，高園便殿火，董仲舒對與此占同」。
Eighth year, eleventh month: Gaoyuan Mausoleum burned. Empress Jia raged unchecked, Jia Mi dominated court—guilt had ripened; both deserved execution. Heaven said: intolerable servants and consorts, however royal, must be cut down—as I scorch Gaoyuan Mausoleum. The feckless emperor spurned Pei Wei and Liu Bian's counsel; the empress and Jia Mi went on to kill the heir. Gan Bao read Gaoyuan's blaze as an answer to the crown prince's deposition. Emperor Wu of Han saw Gao Park's hall burn; Dong Zhongshu's reading matched this sign."
33
，帝納皇后羊氏，-{后}-將入宮，衣中忽有火，眾咸怪之。 ，成都王遂廢-{后}-，處之金墉城。 是後還立，立而復廢者四。 又詔賜死，荀籓表全之。 雖來還在位，然憂逼折辱，終古未聞。 此孽火之應也。
The emperor took Empress Yang; as she entered the palace, flame flickered in her robes—a wonder to all. The Prince of Chengdu deposed her and immured her in Jinyong fortress. She was restored and cast down four times thereafter. Another death edict came; Xun Fan pleaded for her life. Though she sometimes returned to rank, the fear and humiliation were without precedent. Baleful fire had spoken.
34
七月甲午，尚書諸曹火起，延崇禮闥及閣道。 夫百揆王化之本，王者棄法津之應也。 後清河王覃入嗣，不終於位，又殺太子之罰也。
Seventh month, jiawu day: Secretariat bureaus ignited; flames spread to Chongli Gate and the cloister. The hundred offices anchor royal transformation—Heaven answered a ruler who abandoned law. Prince Qinghe Tan succeeded but never finished his mandate—another reckoning for killing an heir.
35
孝懷帝十一月，襄陽火，燒死者三千餘人。 是時王如自號大將軍、司雍二州牧，眾四五萬，攻略郡縣。 此下陵上，陽失其節之應也。
Emperor Huai's eleventh month: Xiangyang burned; three thousand perished in the flames. Wang Ru styled himself grand general and governor of Si and Yong, forty or fifty thousand strong, pillaging towns. Inferiors lording over superiors—yang had lost its pitch.
36
元帝太興中，王敦鎮武昌，武昌災，火起，興眾救之，救於此而發於彼，東西南北數十處俱應，數日不絕。 舊說所謂「濫炎妄起，雖興師眾，不能救之」之謂也。 干寶以為「此臣而君行，亢陽失節，是為王敦陵上，有無君之心，故災也。」
Under Emperor Yuan, Wang Dun at Wuchang faced fire that jumped from spot to spot—dozens of outbreaks across the compass burned for days. Ancient gloss: wildfire everywhere—no army can stamp it out. Gan Bao called it ministers acting as rulers—yang run wild—Wang Dun bullying his sovereign, a heart without liege.
37
正月癸巳，京師大火。 三月，饒安、東光、安陵三縣火，燒七千餘家，死者萬五千人。
First month, guisi day: great fire in the capital. Third month: Rao'an, Dongguang, and Anling burned—seven thousand homes, fifteen thousand dead.
38
明帝正月，京都火。 是時王敦威侮朝廷，多行無禮，內外臣下咸懷怨毒，極陰生陽也。
Emperor Ming's first month: the capital burned. Wang Dun insulted the court and broke protocol; resentment seethed inside and out—extreme yin birthing yang.
39
成帝五月，京師火。
Emperor Cheng's fifth month: capital fire.
40
康帝七月庚申，吳郡災。
Emperor Kang, seventh month, gengshen day: Wu commandery disaster.
41
穆帝六月，震災石季龍太武殿及兩廟端門。 震災月餘乃滅，金石皆盡。 其後季龍死，大亂，遂滅亡。
Emperor Mu's sixth month: lightning shattered Shi Hu's Taiwu Hall and the twin temples' main gates. The lightning lasted over a month; metal and stone melted away. Shi Hu died, chaos followed, and Zhao fell.
42
海西公太和中，郗愔為會稽太守。 六月大旱災，火燒數千家。 延及山陰倉米數百萬斛，炎煙蔽天，不可撲滅。 此亦桓溫強盛，將廢海西，極陰生陽之應也。
Under Duke Haixi, during Taihe, Xi Yin governed Kuaiji. Sixth month drought and fire claimed thousands of homes. Flames reached Shanyin's granaries—millions of hu—smoke veiling the sky, unstoppable. Huan Wen's power was poised to depose Duke Haixi—again extreme yin flashing into yang.
43
孝武帝三月，京師風火大起。 是時桓溫入朝，志在陵上，少主踐位，人懷憂恐，此與太寧火事同。
Emperor Xiaowu's third month: wind-driven fire raged in the capital. Huan Wen entered court bent on dominating the young emperor—fear everywhere, as in the Taining fires.
44
正月，國子學生因風放火，焚房百餘間。 是後考課不厲，賞黜無章。 蓋有育才之名，而無收賢之實，此不哲之罰先兆也。
First month: Imperial Academy students used the wind to torch more than a hundred rooms. Afterward examinations slackened; rewards and dismissals followed no rule. The court cultivated talent in name but not in fact—an early sign of unwisdom's price.
45
十三年十二月乙未，延賢堂災。 是月丙申，螽斯則百堂及客館、驃騎府庫皆災。 于時朝多弊政，衰陵日兆，不哲之罰，皆有象類。 主相不悟，終至亂亡。 會稽王道子寵倖尼及姏母，各樹用其親戚，乃至出入宮掖，禮見人主。 天戒若曰，登延賢堂及客館者多非其人，故災之也。 又，孝武帝更不立皇后，寵倖微賤張夫人，夫人驕妒，皇子不繁，乖「螽斯則百」之道，故災其殿焉。 道子復賞賜不節，故府庫被災，斯亦其罰也。
Thirteenth year, twelfth month, yiwei day: Yanxian Hall burned. Same month, bingshen day: Zhongsi Ze Bai Hall, guest quarters, and the cavalry command depot burned. Court policy rotted and decline showed daily—every unwisdom left its token. Prince and minister slept on until ruin. Prince Daozi of Kuaiji favored nuns and nurses, packing offices with kin who traversed the palace as if equals. Heaven warned: unworthy men filled Yanxian Hall and the guest lodges—so flame purged them. Xiaowudi kept no empress but showered lowborn Lady Zhang—jealous and proud—so heirs were few, mocking the ode's prayer for many sons—the hall answered. Daozi spent the treasury without measure—fire took the stores as payment.
46
安帝三月，龍舟二乘災，是水沴火也。 其後桓玄篡位，帝乃播越。 天戒若曰，王者流遷，不復禦龍舟，故災之耳。
Emperor An's third month: two dragon barges burned—water's revenge on fire. Huan Xuan seized the throne and the emperor fled. Heaven said the wanderer-king would steer no dragon barges—so they burned.
47
八月庚子，尚書下舍曹火。 時桓玄遙錄尚書，故天火，示不復居也。
Eighth month, gengzi day: the lower Secretariat barracks burned. Huan Xuan held the Secretariat by proxy—Heaven's fire said he would not stay.
48
三年，盧循攻略廣州，刺史吳隱之閉城固守。 其十月壬戌夜，火起。 時百姓避寇盈滿城內，隱之懼有應賊者，但務嚴兵，不先救火。 由是府舍焚蕩，燒死者萬餘人，因遂散潰，悉為賊擒。
Third year: Lu Xun besieged Guangzhou; Inspector Wu Yinzi held the walls. Tenth month, renxu night: fire broke out. Refugees packed the town; Yinzi feared traitors and manned the walls instead of fighting the blaze. Administration halls burned; ten thousand died; the defense collapsed and rebels took everyone.
49
七月丁酉，尚書殿中吏部曹火。 九年，京都大火，燒數千家。 十一年，京都所在大行火災，吳界尤甚。 火防甚峻，猶自不絕。 王弘時為吳郡，晝在聽事，見天上有一赤物下，狀如信幡，遙集路南人家屋上，火即大發。 弘知天為之災，故不罪火主。 此帝室衰微之應也。
Seventh month, dingyou day: the Secretariat's personnel bureau burned. Ninth year: capital inferno—thousands of homes lost. The eleventh year saw fires rage across the capital region and even fiercer in Wu. Precautions ran severe; still the blazes would not stop. Prefect Wang Hong, in session by day, watched a red thing fall like a banner and settle on a roof; flame burst forth at once. He read it as Heaven’s work and blamed no householder. The omen matched a fading house of Sima.
50
=
Typographical section divider.
51
土
Earth.
52
=《傳》曰：「修宮室，飾臺榭，內淫亂，犯親戚，侮兄弟，則稼穡不成。」
The gloss: palace-building, terrace ornament, inner debauchery, kin violated, brothers mocked—then the harvest fails.
53
說曰：土，中央，生萬物者也。 其于王者，為內事，宮室、夫婦、親屬，亦相生者也。 古者天子諸侯，宮廟大小高卑有制，-{后}-夫人媵妾多少有度，九族親疏長幼有序。 孔子曰：「禮，與其奢也，寧儉。 」故禹卑宮室，文王刑于寡妻，此聖人之所以昭教化也。 如此，則土得其性矣。 若乃奢淫驕慢，則土失其性。 亡水旱之災而草木百穀不熟，是為稼穡不成。
Earth sits at the center and brings forth all things. For the throne it means the inner realm: halls, marriage, kin—all mutually sustaining. Ancient rulers fixed temple scale, numbered wives and concubines, and ranked the nine agnates. Confucius said: in ritual prefer thrift to waste. Hence Yu’s humble halls and King Wen’s model for his wife—how sages taught the realm. Then earth keeps its true nature. Extravagance, lust, pride, and sloth strip earth of its nature. Without flood or drought, crops still refuse to ripen—that is failure of harvest.
54
吳孫皓時，常歲無水旱，苗稼豐美而實不成，百姓以饑，闔境皆然，連歲不已。 吳人以為傷露，非也。 案劉向《春秋說》曰「水旱當書，不書水旱而曰大無麥禾者，土氣不養，稼穡不成」，此其義也。 皓初遷都武昌，尋還建鄴，又起新館，綴飾珠玉，壯麗過甚，破壞諸營，增廣苑囿，犯暑妨農，官私疲怠。 《月令》，季夏不可以興土功，
Sun Hao’s reign saw fair weather and lush stands that bore no grain—famine everywhere, year on year. Wu blamed dew damage—wrongly. Liu Xiang read the Annals: omitting flood or drought yet recording total crop failure means earth failed to nurture. Hao shifted to Wuchang, came back to Jianye, threw up jeweled halls beyond measure, tore down camps for gardens, worked through summer heat—state and people wore out. The Monthly Ordinance forbids earthworks in late summer—
55
皓皆冒之。 此修宮室飾臺榭之罰也。
Sun Hao broke every rule. Heaven’s sentence for palace-building and terrace finery.
56
元帝，吳郡、吳興、東陽無麥禾，大饑。
Emperor Yuan’s reign: Wu, Wuxing, and Dongyang lost their crops—great famine.
57
成帝，無麥禾，天下大饑。
Emperor Cheng: empire-wide crop failure and famine.
58
穆帝，三麥不登。 十二年，大無麥。
Emperor Mu: three seasons of wheat failed. Twelfth year: almost no wheat.
59
孝武，無麥禾，天下大饑。
Emperor Xiaowu: again no grain empire-wide.
60
安帝，無麥禾，天下大饑。
Emperor An: the same dearth across the land.
61
=
Typographical section divider.
62
金
Metal.
63
=《傳》曰：「好戰攻，輕百姓，飾城郭，侵邊境，則金不從革。」
Love war, despise the people, gild your walls, raid the frontiers—metal then refuses the smith.
64
說曰：金，西方，萬物既成，殺氣之始也。 故立秋而鷹隼擊，秋分而微霜降。 其于王事，出軍行師，把旄杖鉞，誓士眾，抗威武，所以征叛逆，止暴亂也。 《詩》云：「有虔執鉞，如火烈烈。 」又曰：「載戢干戈，載橐弓矢。 」動靜應宜，說以犯難，人忘其死，金得其性矣。 若乃貪欲恣睢，務立威勝，不重人命，則金失其性。 蓋工冶鑄金鐵，冰滯涸堅，不成者眾，乃為變怪，是為金不從革。
Metal is west—the season when growth ends and killing qi begins. Autumn’s start brings raptors; equinox brings first frost. Kings wage war with banners and axes to crush rebels and quell chaos. The Book of Odes: axes raised in awful splendor, fierce as flame. It also says: put away arms and bundle the bows. When war and peace fit the hour and men face peril willingly, metal keeps its nature. Greed for glory, thirst for terror, contempt for life—metal loses its nature. Foundries seize up; castings fail—strange omens of metal refusing the forge.
65
魏時張掖石瑞，雖是晉之符命，而于魏為妖。 好攻戰，輕百姓，飾城郭，侵邊境，魏氏三祖皆有其事。 石圖發于非常之文，此不從革之異也。 晉定大業，多斃曹氏，石瑞文「大討曹」之應也。 案劉歆以《春秋》石言于晉，為金石同類也，是為金不從革，失其性也，劉向以為石白色為主，屬白祥。
Wei’s Zhangye stone foretold Jin yet spelled Wei’s ill omen. Wei’s three founding rulers loved war, neglected the people, dressed their walls, and raided borders. Strange characters on stone chart metal’s refusal to temper. Jin’s victory over Cao answered the stone motto “punish Cao.” Liu Xin linked speaking stone to metal’s stubbornness; Liu Xiang read white stone as a white omen.
66
魏明帝青龍中，盛修宮室，西取長安金狄，承露槃折，聲聞數十里，金狄泣，於是因留霸城。 此金失其性而為異也。
Mingdi’s builders hauled Chang’an’s bronze figures east; the dew tray broke with a roar; statues seemed to weep—left at Ba. Metal had turned unnatural.
67
吳時，曆陽縣有岩穿，似印，咸云「石印封發，天下太平」。 孫皓，印發。 又，陽羨山有石穴，長十餘丈。 皓初修武昌宮，有遷都之意。 是時武昌為離宮。 班固云「離宮與城郭同占」，飾城郭之謂也。 其後，皓出東關，遣丁奉至合肥，皓又大舉出華里，侵邊境之謂也。 故令金失其性，卒面縛而吳亡。
Wu folk saw a seal-shaped pierced rock: “When the stone seal opens, the realm is calm.” Under Sun Hao the seal “opened.” Yangxian’s mountain held a ten-zhang cavern. Sun Hao rebuilt Wuchang palace—capital-move plans. Wuchang served as a secondary palace. Ban Gu equates detached palaces with fortifications—showy ramparts. Sun Hao marched east, sent Ding Fei north—border raids as foretold. Metal’s virtue fled; Sun Hao bound himself and Wu fell.
68
惠帝閏二月，殿前六鐘皆出涕，五刻止。 前年賈后殺楊太后于金墉城，而賈后為惡不止，故鐘出涕，猶傷之也。
Emperor Hui: six court bells wept oil five ke long. After Jia murdered Yang at Jinyong and kept sinning, the bells wept for her.
69
，成都伐長沙，每夜戈戟鋒有火光如懸燭。 此輕人命，好攻戰，金失其性而為光變也。 天戒若曰，兵猶火也，不戢將自焚。 成都不悟，終以敗亡。
When Chengdu struck Changsha, weapon tips flamed nightly like lamps. Contempt for life and love of war turned metal into flickering omens. Heaven warned: armies are fire—unchecked, they consume their masters. Chengdu ignored it and fell.
70
懷帝，項縣有魏豫州刺史賈逵石碑，生金可采，此金不從革而為變也。 五月，汲桑作亂，群寇飆起。
A Wei-era stele sprouted workable gold—metal gone strange. Fifth month: Ji Sang’s revolt and flying bands.
71
清河王覃為世子時，所佩金鈴忽生起如粟者，康王母疑不祥，毀棄之。 及後為惠帝太子，不終於位，卒為司馬越所殺。
Prince Tan’s gold bell grew beads like grain—the dowager smashed it as ill luck. Made crown prince, he never succeeded—Sima Yue slew him.
72
湣帝，石言於平陽。 是時帝蒙塵亦在平陽，故有非言之物而言，妖之大者。 俄而帝為逆胡所弑。
Emperor Min: stone spoke at Pingyang. The captive emperor was there—things that cannot speak spoke; dire portent. Soon barbarian rebels murdered him.
73
元帝，甘卓將襲王敦，既而中止。 及還，家多變怪，照鏡不見其頭。 此金失其性而為妖也。 尋為敦所襲，遂夷滅。
Gan Zhuo planned to strike Wang Dun—then halted. Home filled with marvels; his mirror showed no head. Metal had turned demonic. Wang Dun fell on him and wiped him out.
74
石季龍時，鄴城鳳陽門上金鳳皇二頭飛入漳河。
Shi Hu’s reign: Ye’s gate bronze phoenix heads flew into the Zhang.
75
海西太和中，會稽山陰縣起倉，鑿地得兩大船，滿中錢，錢皆輪文大形。 時日向暮，鑿者馳以告官，官夜遣防守甚嚴。 至明旦，失錢所在，惟有船存。 視其狀，悉有錢處。
Haixi era: digging a granary at Shanyin yielded two treasure boats of large rimmed coins. Dusk fell; diggers raced to magistrates who sealed the site by night. Dawn came—the coins had vanished, boats left empty. Hull scars showed where coin had lain.
76
安帝義熙初，東陽太守殷仲文照鏡不見其頭，尋亦誅翦，占與甘卓同也。
Yixi early: Yin Zhongwen’s mirror showed no head—soon executed like Gan Zhuo.
77
=
Typographical section divider.
78
水
Water.
79
=《傳》曰：「簡宗廟，不禱祠，廢祭祀，逆天時，則水不潤下。」
Neglect shrines, skip sacrifice, defy the seasons—water will not sink to nourish.
80
說曰：水，北方，終藏萬物者也。 其於人道，命終而形藏，精神放越。 聖人為之宗廟，以收魂氣，春秋祭祀，以終孝道。 王者即位，必郊祀天地，禱祈神祇，望秩山川，懷柔百神，亡不宗事。 慎其齋戒，致其嚴敬，是故鬼神歆饗，多獲福助。 此聖王所以順事陰氣，和神人也。 及至發號施令，亦奉天時。 十二月咸得其氣，則陰陽調而終始成。 如此，則水得其性矣。 若乃不敬鬼神，政令逆時，水失其性。 霧水暴出，百川逆溢，壞鄉邑，溺人民，及淫雨傷稼穡，是為水不潤下。
Water is north—the force that seals creation away. For humanity it means death hiding the body while spirit wanders. Sages built shrines to gather souls and seasonal rites to finish filial love. Accession brings suburban rites to Heaven and Earth, prayers to gods, offerings to every peak and stream. Pure vigil and solemn awe win spirits’ favor. Thus sage kings align with yin and join gods and mortals. Their edicts too heed the calendar. Twelve months in harmony—yin and yang complete the cycle. Then water keeps its nature. Spurn spirits and twist policy against the seasons—water loses its way. Flash floods, rivers reversing, towns drowned, endless rains spoiling crops—that is water refusing to soak downward.
81
京房《易傳》曰：「顓事者加，誅罰絕理，厥災水。 其水也，雨，殺人，以隕霜，大風天黃。 饑而不損，茲謂泰，厥大水，水殺人。 避遏有德，茲謂狂，厥水，水流殺人也。 已水則地生蟲。 歸獄不解，茲謂追非，厥水寒，殺人。 追誅不解，茲謂不理，厥水五穀不收。 大敗不解，茲謂皆陰，厥水流入國邑，隕霜殺穀。 」董仲舒曰：「交兵結仇，伏屍流血，百姓愁怨，陰氣盛，故大水也。」
Jing Fang: skewed offices and cruel justice bring water’s scourge. Its form: deadly rains, killing frost, yellow skies and gales. Famine without relent is arrogance—great floods drown the people. Suppressing the worthy is frenzy—rivers kill. After the flood insects breed in the soil. Heaping blame without mercy brings icy killing rains. Endless executions mean misrule—the five grains fail. Total rout unhealed—pure yin—waters flood the capital; frost kills the crop. Dong Zhongshu adds: war breeds feud, corpses litter the ground, the people groan—yin swells—so come the floods.
82
魏文帝六月，大雨霖，伊洛溢，至津陽城門，漂數千家，殺人。 初，帝即位，自鄴遷洛，營造宮室，而不起宗廟。 太祖神主猶在鄴，嘗於建始殿饗祭如家人禮，終黃初不復還鄴。 又郊社神祇，未有定位。 此簡宗廟廢祭祀之罰也。
Wei Emperor Wen’s sixth month brought ceaseless rain; the Yi and Luo poured through Jinyang Gate, washing away thousands of homes. On his accession he moved the court from Ye to Luoyang, lavishing palaces while erecting no ancestral shrine. His father’s tablet stayed in Ye while he feasted the dead like a private household in Jianshi Hall—never restoring proper site through the Huangchu era. Heaven-and-earth spirits lacked fixed stations at the suburban shrines. Heaven’s sentence for shrines scanted and offerings abandoned.
83
吳孫權夏，茶陵縣鴻水溢出，漂二百餘家。 十三年秋，丹陽、故鄣等縣又鴻水溢出。 案權稱帝三十年，竟不於建鄴創七廟。 惟父堅一廟遠在長沙，而郊祀禮闕。 嘉禾初，群臣奏宜郊祀，又不許。 末年雖一南郊，而北郊遂無聞焉。 吳楚之望亦不見秩，反祀羅陽妖神，以求福助。 天戒若曰，權簡宗廟，不禱祠，廢祭祀，故示此罰，欲其感悟也。
Sun Quan's reign: the Hong torrent burst Chaling county and swept away two hundred homes. Autumn of the thirteenth year: Danyang and Guchang saw the same flood surge. Sun Quan ruled three decades as emperor yet never founded the seven royal shrines at Jianye. Only Sun Jian's lone shrine stood distant in Changsha; suburban worship stayed neglected. Early in Jiahe ministers urged suburban rites—Sun Quan refused. Late in life he performed one southern suburban rite but never paired it with the northern altar. He skipped ranked sacrifices to the great peaks and worshipped freak gods at Luoyang for luck. Heaven warned: shrines scanted, prayers neglected, offerings dropped—the floods were meant to wake him.
84
，吳又有大風湧水之異。 是冬，權南郊，宜是鑒咎徵乎！ 還而寢疾，明年四月薨。 一曰，權時信納譖訴，雖陸遜勳重，子和儲貳，猶不得其終，與漢安帝聽讒免楊震、廢太子同事也。 且赤烏中無年不用兵，百姓愁怨。 八年秋，將軍馬茂等又圖逆。
Wu also saw gales and walls of water. That winter he offered the southern suburban—perhaps answering the prior portent. He took ill on his return and died the next spring. Some blame Sun Quan's taste for slander—Lu Xun and heir Sun He ruined like Han Andi's purge of Yang Zhen. The Chiwu era knew war every year and endless popular resentment. That autumn Ma Mao and fellow officers plotted revolt.
85
魏明帝九月，淫雨，冀、兗、徐、豫四州水出，沒溺殺人，漂失財產。 帝自初即位，便淫奢極欲，多占幼女，或奪士妻，崇飾宮室，妨害農戰，觸情恣欲，至是彌甚，號令逆時，饑不損役。 此水不潤下之應也。 吳孫亮夏，大水。 亮即位四年，乃立權廟。 又終吳世不上祖宗之號，不修嚴父之禮，昭穆之數有闕。 亮及休、皓又並廢二郊，不秩群神。 此簡宗廟不祭祀之罰也。 又，是時孫峻專政，陰勝陽之應乎！
Wei Emperor Ming's ninth month: soaking rains drowned Ji, Yan, Xu, and Yu. Since accession he hoarded girls, seized wives, lavished palaces, crippled farming and defense—commands ran against the seasons while famine raged and corvée never eased. That is water refusing to nourish below. Sun Liang's summer brought catastrophic flooding. Four years into his reign Sun Liang finally built a shrine for Sun Quan. Through Wu's reign they never titled the ancestors or performed full father rites—the shrine ranks stayed broken. Sun Liang, Sun Xiu, and Sun Hao each scrapped both suburb sacrifices and left gods unordered. Heaven punished neglected shrines and empty altars. Sun Jun's dictatorship matched yin overwhelming yang.
86
孫休五月，大雨，水泉湧溢。 昔歲作浦裏塘，功費無數，而田不可成，士卒死叛，或自賊殺，百姓愁怨，陰氣盛也。 休又專任張布，退盛沖等，吳人賊之應也。 五年八月壬午，大雨震電，水泉湧溢。
Sun Xiu's fifth month: downpours until springs burst their banks. The costly Pulitang canal brought only waste fields, mutinous troops, and popular despair—yin rose thick. Sun Xiu relied solely on Zhang Bu and cashiered Sheng Chong—the people of Wu paid the price. Fifth year, eighth month, renwu: thunder, cloudbursts, and boiling springs.
87
武帝九月，青、徐、兗、豫四州大水。 七年六月，大雨霖，河、洛、伊、沁皆溢，殺二百餘人。 自帝即尊位，不加三后祖宗之號。 又除明堂南郊五帝座，同稱昊天上帝，一位而已。 又省先-{后}-配地之祀。 此簡宗廟廢祭祀之罰也。
Emperor Wu's ninth month: Qing, Xu, Yan, and Yu drowned. Seventh year, sixth month: the He, Luo, Yi, and Qin rivers burst their banks, killing hundreds. Since enthronement he gave no posthumous ranks to the three empresses or forebears. He stripped the Ming Hall of the five polar gods and collapsed worship into one Haotian seat. He dropped the rite pairing the late empress with Earth. Heaven's sentence for shrines scanted and offerings abandoned.
88
咸甯元年九月，徐州大水。 二年七月癸亥，河南、魏郡暴水，殺百餘人。 閏月，荊州郡國五大水，流四千餘家。 去年采擇良家子女，露面入殿，帝親簡閱，務在姿色，不訪德行，有蔽匿者以不敬論，搢紳愁怨，天下非之，陰盛之應也。
Xianning year one, ninth month: Xuzhou floods. Year two, seventh month, guihai: Henan and Wei commanderies drowned a hundred souls. Intercalary month: five Jingzhou jurisdictions lost four thousand households to the torrent. Palace draft chose women by face alone; hiding beauty earned indictment—the elite groaned and yin energies swelled.
89
三年六月，益、梁二州郡國八暴水，殺三百餘人。 七月，荊州大水。 九月，始平郡大水。 十月，青、徐、兗、豫、荊、益、梁七州又大水。 是時賈充等用事專恣，而正人疏外者多，陰氣盛也。
Third year, sixth month: Yi and Liang lost eight counties and three hundred lives. Seventh month: Jingzhou inundated. Ninth month: Shiping commandery flooded. Tenth month: seven provinces from Qing to Liang flooded again. Jia Chong's clique ran riot while honest officials sat outside—yin dominated.
90
四年七月，司、冀、兗、豫、荊、揚郡國二十大水，傷秋稼，壞屋室，有死者。
Fourth year, seventh month: twenty jurisdictions from Si to Yang drowned crops and homes.
91
六月，泰山、江夏大水，泰山流三百家，殺六十餘人，江夏亦殺人。 時平吳後，王浚為元功而詆劾妄加，荀、賈為無謀而並蒙重賞，收吳姬五千，納之後宮，此其應也。
Sixth month: Taishan and Jiangxia surged—three hundred Taishan homes gone, sixty dead; Jiangxia too took lives. Peace with Wu brought Wang Jun slandered, Xun and Jia rewarded without merit, and five thousand Wu women swept into the harem—the floods answered that hubris.
92
四年七月，兗州大水。 十二月，河南及荊、揚六州大水。 五年九月，郡國四大水，又隕霜。 是月，南安等五郡大水。 六年四月，郡國十大水，壞廬舍。 七年九月，郡國八大水。 八月六月，郡國八大水。
Fourth year, seventh month: Yanzhou flood. Twelfth month: Henan plus six provinces from Jing to Yang drowned. Fifth year, ninth month: four jurisdictions flooded and frost fell. Same month: Nan'an circuit and five commanderies inundated. Sixth year, fourth month: ten jurisdictions wrecked farmsteads. Seventh year, ninth month: eight jurisdictions underwater. The text's corrupted date still records another wave of flooding in eight jurisdictions.
93
惠帝，有水災。 五年五月，潁川、淮南大水。 六月，城陽、東莞大水，殺人，荊、揚、徐、兗、豫五州又水。 是時帝即位已五載，猶未郊祀，其蒸嘗亦多不親行事。 此簡宗廟廢祭祀之罰。
Emperor Hui's reign brought repeated inundations. Fifth year, fifth month: Yingchuan and Huainan flooded. Sixth month: Chengyang and Dongguan drowned people; Jing, Yang, Xu, Yan, and Yu flooded again. Five years on the throne he still skipped suburban worship and often sent substitutes to seasonal feasts. Heaven punished shrines neglected and offerings abandoned.
94
六年五月，刑、揚二州大水。 是時賈后亂朝，寵樹賈、郭，女主專政，陰氣盛之應也。
Sixth year, fifth month: the Jing and Yang circuits drowned. Empress Jia's faction ruled through female favorites—yin's surge.
95
八年五月，金墉城井溢。 《漢志》，成帝時有此妖，後王莽僭逆。 今有此妖，趙王倫篡位，倫廢帝於此城，井溢所在，其天意也。 九月，荊、揚、徐、冀、豫五州大水。 是時賈后暴戾滋甚，韓謐驕猜彌扇，卒害太子，旋以禍滅。 九年四月，宮中井水沸溢。
Eighth year, fifth month: Jinyong's well boiled over. Han records match Chengdi's well omen with Wang Mang's usurpation. The same sign preceded Sima Lun's coup—the deposed emperor sat in Jinyong where the water rose. Ninth month: five provinces from Jing to Yu submerged. Jia Nanfeng turned brutal, Han Mi grew vicious—the heir died and they followed. Ninth year, fourth month: palace wells gushed.
96
永甯元年七月，南陽、東海大水。 是時齊王冏專政，陰盛之應也。
Yongning year one, seventh month: Nanyang and Donghai floods. Sima Jiong's dictatorship showed yin ascendant.
97
七月，兗、豫、徐、冀四州水。 時將相力政，無尊主心，陰盛故也。
Seventh month: Yan, Yu, Xu, and Ji awash. Warlords feuded with no loyalty to the throne—again yin rising.
98
孝懷帝四月，江東大水。 時王導等潛懷翼戴之計，陰氣盛也。
Emperor Huai's fourth month drowned east of the Yangzi. Wang Dao's circle plotted a new emperor—another yin tide.
99
元帝六月，大水。 是時王敦內懷不臣，傲很陵上，此陰氣盛也。 四年七月，又大水。
Emperor Yuan's sixth month: widespread flood. Wang Dun nursed treason and bullied the court—yin ruled. Fourth year, seventh month: floods returned.
100
五月，荊州及丹陽、宣城、吳興、壽春大水。
Fifth month: Jingzhou and four eastern commanderies flooded.
101
明帝五月，丹陽、宣城、吳興、壽春大水。 是時王敦威權震主，陰氣盛故也。
Emperor Ming's fifth month repeated the eastern inundations. Wang Dun's terror tactics cowed the emperor—yin still dominant.
102
成帝五月，大水。 是時嗣主幼沖，母后稱制，庾亮以元舅決事禁中，陰勝陽故也。
Emperor Cheng's fifth month: deluge. A child throne, empress regent, Yu Liang ruling from the harem—yin eclipsed yang.
103
二年五月戊子，京都大水。 是冬，以蘇峻稱兵，都邑塗地。
Second year, fifth month, wuzi: the capital drowned. That winter Su Jun's revolt left the capital in ashes and mud.
104
四年七月，丹陽、宣城、吳興、會稽大水。 是冬，郭默作亂，荊豫共討之，半歲乃定，兵役之應也。
Fourth year, seventh month: the lower Yangzi basin flooded. Guo Mo's winter rebellion took Jing and Yu half a year to crush—war's echo.
105
七年五月，大水。 是時帝未親機務，政在大臣，陰勝陽也。
Seventh year, fifth month: flood. The emperor stayed clear of statecraft—ministers held yin sway.
106
八月，長沙、武陵大水。
Eighth month: Changsha and Wuling submerged.
107
穆帝五月，大水。 五年五月，大水。 六年五月，又大水。 時幼主沖弱，母后臨朝，又將相大臣各執權政，與咸和初同事也。
Emperor Mu's fifth month: inundation. Fifth year, fifth month: flood. Sixth year, fifth month: floods again. Another child ruler, another regent, another crop of strongmen—like Xianhe's opening years.
108
七年七月甲辰夜，濤水入石頭，死者數百人。 是時殷浩以私忿廢蔡謨，遐邇非之。 又幼主在上而殷桓交惡，選徒聚甲，各崇私權，陰勝陽之應也。 一說，濤水入石頭，以為兵占。 是後殷浩、桓溫、謝尚、荀羨連年征伐，百姓愁怨也。
Seventh year, seventh month, jiachen night: a bore swept Shitou fort—hundreds drowned. Yin Hao cashiered Cai Mo from spite—the realm jeered. Child on the throne; Yin Hao and Huan Wen feuded—hosts mobilized for private ends. Some read the Shitou tide as an omen of war. Yin Hao, Huan Wen, Xie Shang, and Xun Xian kept the realm at war until the people groaned.
109
五月，大水。 五年四月，又大水。 是時桓溫權制朝廷，專征伐，陰勝陽也。
The fifth month brought another deluge. The fifth year’s fourth month flooded again. Huan Wen hijacked the government for foreign wars—yin eclipsed yang.
110
海西六月，京師大水，平地數尺，浸及太廟。 硃雀大航纜斷，三艘流入大江。 丹陽、晉陵、吳郡、吳興、臨海五郡又大水，稻稼蕩沒，黎庶饑饉。 初，四年桓溫北伐敗績，十喪其九，五年又征淮南，逾歲乃克，百姓愁怨之應也。
Haixi’s sixth month drowned the capital knee-deep and lapped the ancestral shrine. The Vermilion Bird bridge parted; three hulls washed into the Yangzi. Five eastern commanderies flooded again; grain vanished and famine spread. Huan Wen’s failed northern thrust and grinding Huainan war answered popular resentment.
111
簡文帝十二月壬午，濤水入石頭。 明年，妖賊盧竦率其屬數百人入殿，略取武庫三庫甲仗，遊擊將軍毛安之討滅之，兵興、陰盛之應也。
Emperor Jianwen’s twelfth month, renwu day: the bore reached Shitoe. Lu Song raided the palace armory; Mao Anzhi crushed him—another war omen.
112
孝武帝六月，大水。 是時帝幼弱，政在將相。 五年五月，大水。 六年六月，揚、荊、江三州大水。 八年三月，始興、南康、廬陵大水，平地五丈。 十年五月，大水。 自八年破苻堅後，有事中州，役無寧歲，愁怨之應也。
Emperor Xiaowu’s sixth month: floods. A boy emperor left policy to generals and ministers. Fifth month: inundation. Sixth month: Yang, Jing, and Jiang drowned. Third month, eighth year: western commanderies stood fifteen feet under water. Tenth year, fifth month: flood. Campaigns on the Central Plain never ceased after Feishui—popular anger answered in rain.
113
十三年十二月，濤水入石頭，毀大航，殺人。 明年，慕容氏寇擾司兗，鎮戍西北，疲於奔命，愁怨之應也。
Thirteenth year: Shitou tide snapped the great pontoon and killed. Murong incursions wore out the northwest—Heaven echoed with floods.
114
十五年七月，沔中諸郡及兗州大水。 是時緣河紛爭，征戍勤瘁之應也。
Fifteenth year, seventh month: Han basin and Yanzhou underwater. Frontier armies along the Han were spent—waters rose in reply.
115
十七年六月甲寅，濤水入石頭，毀大航，漂船舫，有死者。 京口西浦亦濤入殺人。 永嘉郡潮水湧起，近海四縣人多死。 後四年帝崩，而王恭再攻京師，京師亦發眾以禦之，兵彼頻興，百姓愁怨之應也。
Seventeenth year, jiayin: Shitou tide wrecked the bridge and hulls. Jingkou’s west landing drowned too. Yongjia’s tidal bore drowned four counties. Four years on the emperor fell; Wang Gong’s sieges and counter-mobilizations matched the floods.
116
十八年六月己亥，始興、南康、廬陵大水，深五丈。 十九年七月，荊徐大水，傷秋稼。 二十年六月，荊徐又大水。 二十一年五月癸卯，大水。 是時政事多弊，兆庶非之。
Eighteenth year, jihai: the three southern commanderies sank five zhang deep. Nineteenth year: Jing and Xu spoiled the harvest. Twentieth year: Jing and Xu flooded again. Twenty-first year, guimao: deluge. Policy rotted and the people muttered.
117
安帝五月，荊州大水，平地三丈。 去年殷仲堪舉兵向京師，是年春又殺郗恢，陰盛作威之應也。 仲堪尋亦敗亡。
Emperor An’s fifth month sank Jingzhou ten feet deep. Yin Zhongkan’s march on the capital and murder of Xi Hui drew the flood. Zhongkan fell soon after.
118
五年五月，大水。 是時會稽王世子元顯作威陵上，又桓玄擅西夏，孫恩亂東國，陰勝陽之應也。
Fifth month: flood. Sima Yuanxian bullied the throne; Huan Xuan held the west; Sun En tore the east—yin ruled.
119
十二月，桓玄篡位。 其明年二月庚寅夜，濤水入石頭。 商旅方舟萬計，漂敗流斷，骸胔相望。 江左雖頻有濤變，未有若斯之甚。 三月，義軍克京都，玄敗走，遂夷滅之。
Twelfth month: Huan Xuan took the throne. Next year, gengyin night: Shitou tide. Countless merchant hulls shattered; corpses choked the shore. Jiangnan had seen surges—never this fierce. Third month: loyal troops retook Jiankang; Huan Xuan fell.
120
三年二月己丑朔夜，濤水入石頭，漂沒殺人，大航流敗。
Third year, jichou night: Shitou drowned folk and ruined the bridge.
121
十二月己未，濤水入石頭。 二年十二月己未夜，濤水入石頭。 明年，駱球父環潛結桓胤、殷仲文等謀作亂，劉稚亦謀反，凡所誅滅數十家。
Twelfth month, jiwei: Shitou tide. Second year, jiwei night: another Shitou surge. Next year Luo Huan’s plot with Yin Zhongwen and Liu Zhi’s coup wiped dozens of families.
122
三年五月丙午，大水。 四年十二月戊寅，濤水入石頭。 明年，王旅北討。
Third year, fifth month, bingwu: flood. Fourth year, wuyin: Shitou tide. Imperial armies marched north the next year.
123
六年五月丁巳，大水。 乙丑，盧循至蔡洲。
Sixth year, dingsi: deluge. Yichou: Lu Xun anchored at Cai Isle.
124
八年六月，大水。 九年五月辛巳，大水。 十年五月丁丑，大水。 戊寅，西明門地穿，湧水出，毀門扇及限，亦水沴土也。 七月乙丑，淮北風災，大水殺人。 十一年七月丙戌，大水，淹漬太廟，百官赴救。 明年，王旅北討關河。
Eighth year, sixth month: flood. Ninth year, xinsi: flood. Tenth year, dingchou: flood. Wuyin: Ximing Gate split open and spouted—water drowning earth. Seventh month, yichou: Huabei gale and flood. Eleventh year, bingxu: flood reached the temple; officials scrambled to save it. Next year the northern expedition crossed Guanhe.
125
敬用五事
The five comportments.
126
《經》曰：「敬用五事：一曰貌，二曰言，三曰視，四曰聽，五曰思。 貌曰恭，言曰從，視曰明，聽曰聰，思曰睿。 恭作肅，從作乂，明作哲，聰作謀，睿作聖。 休徵：曰肅，時雨若； 乂，時晹若； 哲，時燠若； 謀，時寒若； 聖，時風若。 咎徵：曰狂，恆雨若； 僭，恆晹若； 豫，恆燠若； 急，恆寒若； {雨瞀}，恆風若。」
The canon lists five human gauges: bearing, words, sight, hearing, thought. Bearing must be respectful; speech obedient; vision lucid; hearing sharp; thought clear. From those virtues come order, wisdom, counsel, and sage rule. Auspice of sobriety: seasonable rain. Order brings fair skies. Wisdom brings gentle warmth. Counsel brings winter discipline. Sageliness brings winds in season. Insolence summons endless rain. Presumption brings drought glare. Complacency breeds muggy heat. Rashness locks the realm in cold. Obstruction aloft means ceaseless wind.
127
《傳》曰：「貌之不恭，是謂不肅，厥咎狂，厥罰恆雨，厥極惡。 時則有服妖，時則有龜孽，時則有雞禍，時則有下體生上之痾，時則有青眚青祥。 惟金沴木。」
The gloss: disrespectful bearing breaks solemnity; madness follows; endless rain is its price. Hence costume freaks, turtle omens, cock disasters, upside-down flesh, green blights. Metal injures wood in the cycle.
128
說曰：凡草木之類謂之妖。 妖猶夭胎，言尚微也。 蟲豸之類謂之孽。 孽則芽孽矣。 及六畜，謂之禍，言其著也。 及人，謂之痾。 痾，病貌也，言浸深也。 甚則有異物生，謂之眚； 自外來，謂之祥。 祥，猶禎也。 氣相傷，謂之沴。 沴猶臨蒞，不和意也。 每一事云「時則」以絕之，言非必俱至，或有或亡，或在前或在後。 孝武時，夏侯始昌通《五經》，善推《五行傳》，以傳族子夏侯勝，下及許商，皆以教所賢弟子。 其傳與劉向同，惟劉歆傳獨異。
Plant anomalies are called yao. “Prodigy” implies incipient strangeness. Crawling things misbred are nie. Portents sprout like buds. When beasts show it, call it huo—clear for all to see. When humans show it, call it e—malformation. “E” marks sickness working inward. Extremes breed freak objects—qing calamities. Outsiders bring xiang omens. Xiang parallels blessing. When qi wounds qi, call it li. Mutual sustainment is harmony. Each clause adds “when in season” to stress omens need not arrive together. Xiahou Shichang’s cosmology passed to Xiahou Sheng and Xu Shang’s schools. Their gloss matched Liu Xiang; Liu Xin alone diverged.
129
貌之不恭，是謂不肅。 肅，敬也。 內曰恭，外曰敬。 人君行己，體貌不恭，怠慢驕蹇，則不能敬萬事，失則狂易，故其咎狂也。 上慢下暴，則陰氣勝，故其罰常雨也。 水傷百穀，衣食不足，則奸宄並作，故其極惡也。
Disrespectful bearing breaks solemnity. Solemnity is reverence. Inner life shows as gong; outer shows as jing. Rulers who slouch and sneer cannot honor creation—madness is their fault. Loose thrones and cruel subjects swell yin—hence endless rain. Floods spoil grain; want breeds crime—that evil is the extreme.
130
一曰，人多被刑，或形貌醜惡，亦是也。 風俗狂慢，變節易度，則為剽輕奇怪之服，故有服妖。 水類動，故有龜孽。 于《易》，《巽》為雞。 雞有冠、距，文武之貌。 而不為威，貌氣毀，故有雞禍。 一曰，水歲多雞死及為怪，亦是也。 上失威儀，則有強臣害君上者，故有下體生於上之痾。 木色青，故有青眚青祥。 凡貌傷者病木氣，木氣病則金沴之，沖氣相通也。 于《易》，《震》在東方，為春為木； 《兌》在西方，為秋為金； 《離》在南方，為夏為火； 《坎》在北方，為冬為水。 春與秋日夜分，寒暑平，是以金木之氣易以相變，故貌傷則致秋陰常雨，言傷則致春陽常旱也。 至於冬夏，日夜相反，寒暑殊絕，水火之氣不得相並，故視傷常燠、聽傷常寒者，其氣然也。 逆之，其極曰惡； 順之，其福曰攸好德。 劉歆《貌傳》曰有鱗蟲之孽，羊禍，鼻痾。 說以為于天文東方辰為龍星，故為鱗蟲。 于《易》，《兌》為羊，木為金所病，故致羊禍，與常雨同應。 此說非是。 春與秋氣陰陽相敵，木病金盛，故能相並，惟此一事耳。 禍與妖痾祥眚同類，不得獨異。
Some read it as mass punishments or grotesque faces. Fashion turns reckless—odd dress follows. Water forces twitch—turtle omens hatch. The Zhou yi maps Xun to fowl. Cocks bear crown and spur—tokens of wen and wu. Without majesty its bearing fails—hence cock disasters. Another gloss holds that water-phase years bring mass deaths among fowl and strange portents—and that belongs here as well. When superiors forfeit proper bearing, strong ministers wound the ruler—which yields the prodigy of “lower members sprouting on the upper body.” Wood’s hue is green, which is why green blights and green omens appear. Whenever demeanor falters, the wood phase suffers; when wood ails, metal strikes it—the two opposing forces interact. In the Book of Changes, the trigram Zhen is placed in the east—it signifies spring and wood. Dui belongs to the west—it signifies autumn and metal. Li belongs to the south—it signifies summer and fire. Kan belongs to the north—it signifies winter and water. Spring and autumn balance day and night and level cold with heat, so metal and wood readily trade influence—thus impaired bearing yields endless autumn rains, while impaired speech yields spring drought beneath a glaring sun. Winter and summer invert day and night and separate cold from heat so sharply that water and fire cannot mingle—so impaired sight trends warm and impaired hearing trends cold: that is how their phases behave. Defy the pattern, and the extreme is named evil. Follow it, and the blessing is “delight in virtue.” Liu Xin’s Treatise on Bearing lists prodigies among scaly creatures, sheep omens, and nasal deformities. The gloss identifies the eastern asterism chen as the Dragon Star—hence “scaly creatures.” In the Changes Dui signifies sheep; wood falls ill to metal—hence sheep calamities that align with ceaseless rain. That reading is wrong. Only in spring and autumn do yin and yang contend as equals, with enfeebled wood under dominant metal, so the phases can combine—nowhere else. Calamities sit on the same spectrum as prodigies, lesions, omens, and blights—you cannot set them apart.
131
魏尚書鄧颺揚行步馳縱，筋不束體，坐起傾倚，若無手足，此貌之不恭也。 管輅謂之鬼躁。 鬼躁者，凶終之徵，後卒誅也。
Deng Yang of Wei, a Secretariat director, walked with a loose, racing stride—his sinews seemed not to hold his body; he slumped when he sat or rose as though limbless: irreverence of demeanor. Guan Lu dubbed it “demon restlessness.” “Ghost restlessness” foretells a bloody finish—he was put to death in the end.
132
惠帝元康中，貴遊子弟相與為散發倮身之飲，對弄婢妾，逆之者傷好，非之者負譏，希世之士恥不與焉。 蓋貌之不恭，胡狄侵中國之萌也。 其後遂有五胡之亂，此又失在狂也。
Under Emperor Hui in the Yuan-kang years, young aristocrats threw banquets with hair unbound and skins naked, fondling servant girls in plain sight; crossing them cost goodwill, criticizing them earned jeers, and career-minded men were ashamed to stay away. It was bearing without dignity—the first stirrings of steppe peoples overrunning China. The Five Hu upheaval followed—another case of the “madness” failing.
133
元康中，賈謐親貴，數入二宮，與儲君遊戲，無降下心。 又嘗因弈棋爭道，成都王穎厲色曰：「皇太子國之儲貳，賈謐何敢無禮！ 」謐猶不悛，故及於禍，貌不恭之罰也。
During Yuan-kang, Jia Mi enjoyed imperial favor: he kept slipping into the two palaces to amuse the crown prince and never lowered himself in deference. Once, disputing a chess placement, Sima Ying, Prince of Chengdu, snapped: “The crown prince is the realm’s reserve—how dare Jia Mi lack respect! ” Yet Jia Mi refused to mend his ways and paid with his life—the reckoning for disrespectful bearing.
134
齊王冏既誅趙王倫，因留輔政，坐拜百官，符敕臺府，淫醟專驕，不一朝覲，此狂恣不肅之咎也。 天下莫不高其功而慮其亡也，冏終弗改，遂致夷滅。
After killing Prince Zhao Sima Lun, Prince Qi Sima Jiong stayed as regent: he handed out posts from his seat, ran the ministries by decree, reveled in wine and pride, and skipped every audience—mad impudence with no dignity. The realm praised his deed yet feared his fall; Jiong never changed—and was wiped out.
135
司馬道子於府園內列肆，使姬人酤鬻，身自貿易。 干寶以為貴者失位，降在皁隸之象也。 俄而道子見廢，以庶人終，此貌不恭之應也。
Sima Daozi lined his estate with shops, put concubines behind the counter, and haggled himself. Gan Bao read it as rank pulled down among common hirelings. Daozi was soon stripped of office and died a commoner—the sign answering irreverent bearing.
136
安帝，將拜授劉毅世子，毅以王命之重，當設饗宴，親請吏佐臨視。 至拜日，國僚不重白，默拜於廄中。 王人將反命，毅方知之，大以為恨，免郎中令劉敬叔官。 天戒若曰，此惰略嘉禮不肅之妖也。 其後毅遂被殺焉。
When Emperor An was to ennoble Liu Yi’s heir, Liu Yi—because the imperial commission mattered—should have spread a banquet and brought his staff to witness it. Come the ceremony, his officers never cleared it upstairs; they muttered the investiture inside the stables. The imperial messenger was nearly on the road back before Liu Yi heard—he was furious and cashiered Liu Jingshu, director of the gentlemen-of-the-palace. Heaven warned: skimping on a sacred ceremony without gravity yields this portent. Liu Yi was executed soon after.
137
庶征恆雨，劉歆以為《春秋》大雨，劉向以為大水。
Under “miscellaneous omens,” endless rain: Liu Xin reads the Spring and Autumn’s “great rains”; Liu Xiang reads catastrophic flood.
138
魏明帝秋，數大雨，多暴卒，雷電非常，至殺鳥雀。 案楊阜上疏，此恆雨之罰也。 時天子居喪不哀，出入弋獵無度，奢侈繁興，奪農時，故水失其性而恆雨為罰。
One autumn under Wei’s Mingdi the skies opened repeatedly; people dropped dead; lightning flashed unnaturally, killing even small birds. Yang Fu’s memorial treats it as the scourge of ceaseless rain. The emperor wore mourning without grief, hunted without restraint, lavished wealth, and stole time from the fields—water lost its proper character, and unending rain was the penalty.
139
八月，大雨霖三十餘日，伊、洛、河、漢皆溢，歲以凶饑。
For over thirty days in the eighth month torrents fell; the Yi, Luo, Yellow River, and Han burst their banks; the harvest failed and hunger spread.
140
吳孫亮二月甲寅，大雨，震電。 乙卯，雪，大寒。 案劉歆說，此時當雨而不當大，大雨，恆雨之罰也。 於始震電之，明日而雪，大寒，又常寒之罰也。 劉向以為既已雷電，則雪不當復降，皆失時之異也。 天戒若曰，為君失時，賊臣將起。 先震電而後雪者，陰見間隙，起而勝陽，逆弑之禍將成也。 亮不悟，尋見廢。 此與《春秋》魯隱同。
On jiayin of the second month under Wu’s Sun Liang came deluges and lightning. The next day, yimao: snow and bitter cold. Liu Xin argues it should have sprinkled then—a deluge instead marks the “constant rain” scourge. Lightning first, then snow and killing frost the day after—another stroke of “constant cold.” Liu Xiang thought lightning should rule out more snow—each event arrived out of season. Heaven warned: mistiming sovereignty breeds rebellious ministers. Lightning then snow means yin spied a gap, surged, and mastered yang—the blade and coup draw near. Sun Liang never saw it—soon he was cast down. It parallels the Spring and Autumn record for Duke Yin of Lu.
141
武帝六月，大雨霖。 甲辰，河、洛、伊、沁水同時並溢，流四千九百餘家，殺二百餘人，沒秋稼千三百六十餘頃。
In Emperor Wu’s sixth month the rains would not stop. On jiachen the Yellow River, Luo, Yi, and Qin floods crested as one, washing away nearly five thousand homes, killing over two hundred, and drowning more than 1,360 qing of autumn grain.
142
七月，任城、梁國暴雨，害豆麥。 九月，南安郡霖雨暴雪，樹木摧折，害秋稼。 是秋，魏郡西平郡九縣、淮南、平原霖雨暴水，霜傷秋稼。
In the seventh month Ren-cheng and Liang were hit by cloudbursts that ruined beans and wheat. Nan-an commandery endured weeks of rain and blizzard that shattered trees and spoiled the autumn harvest. That fall, nine counties across Wei and Xi-ping along with Huai-nan and Ping-yuan were flooded; late frost ruined the crops.
143
惠帝十月、義陽、南陽、東海霖雨，淹害秋麥。
In Emperor Hui’s tenth month relentless rain swamped Yi-yang, Nan-yang, and Dong-hai and drowned the winter wheat.
144
元帝，春雨至於夏。 是時王敦執權，不恭之罰也。
Under Emperor Yuan spring rains dragged into summer. Wang Dun held the reins then—the penalty for irreverent bearing.
145
，春雨四十餘日，晝夜雷電震五十餘日。 是時王敦興兵，王師敗績之應也。
For over forty days spring rains fell; thunder rolled night and day for more than fifty. Wang Dun was marching then—the omen of the imperial army’s rout.
146
成帝，春雨五十餘日，恆雷電。 是時雖斬蘇峻，其餘黨猶據守石頭，至其滅後，淫雨乃霽。
Emperor Cheng’s reign brought fifty-odd days of spring rain and ceaseless thunder. Su Jun was dead but his followers still held Stone City; only when they were wiped out did the endless rain break.
147
八月乙丑，荊州之長沙攸、醴陵、武陵之龍陽，三縣雨水，浮漂屋室，殺人，損秋稼。 是時帝幼，權在於下。
On yichou in the eighth month, downpours in You (Chang-sha), Li-ling, and Long-yang (Wu-ling) swept away homes, took lives, and ruined the autumn harvest. The sovereign was a child; real power sat beneath the throne.
148
=
Typographical section divider.
149
服妖
Garment omens.
150
=魏武帝以天下凶荒，資財乏匱，始擬古皮弁，裁縑帛為白帢，以易舊服。 傅玄曰； 「白乃軍容，非國容也。 」干寶以為「縞素，凶喪之象也」。 名之為帢，毀辱之言也，蓋革代之後，劫殺之妖也。
Emperor Wu of Wei, with the realm starving and supplies exhausted, copied the old leather bonnet and tailored plain silk into a white qia to replace court headgear. Fu Xuan observed: “White belongs on campaign, not in state ritual. ” Gan Bao read it as “bleached cloth signals bereavement.” Calling it a qia was mockery—a portent of usurpation and bloodshed after the throne changed hands.
151
魏明帝著繡帽，披縹紈半袖，常以見直臣楊阜，諫曰：「此禮何法服邪！ 」帝默然。 近服妖也。 夫縹，非禮之色。 褻服尚不以紅紫，況接臣下乎？ 人主親禦非法之章，所謂自作孽不可禳也。 帝既不享永年，身沒而祿去王室，後嗣不終，遂亡天下。
Mingdi of Wei sported an embroidered hat and a sky-blue half-sleeve; he wore them to see the upright Yang Fu, who protested: “What canonical garment is this! ” The emperor had no reply. It skirted a garment omen. Sky-blue is not a ritual hue. Undress eschews forbidden reds and purples—how dare court robes flout them before ministers? When the sovereign dons unlawful regalia, he courts a doom no rite can lift. He gained no long reign; dead, his line lost the mandate—his heirs did not endure, and the realm slipped away.
152
，發銅鑄為巨人二，號曰翁仲，置之司馬門外。 案古長人見，為國亡。 長狄見臨洮，為秦亡之禍。 始皇不悟，反以為嘉祥，鑄銅人以象之。 魏法亡國之器，而於義竟無取焉。 蓋服妖也。
Bronze was recast into two colossal statues dubbed Wengzhong and set outside the Sima Gate. Ancient precedent says giants foretell a kingdom’s end. The Long Di at Lintao spelled Qin’s doom. The First Emperor misread the sign as blessing and cast bronze giants in their likeness. Wei copied a dying dynasty’s stunt—to no moral purpose. Another garment omen.
153
尚書何晏好服婦人之服，傅玄曰：「此妖服也。 夫衣裳之制，所以定上下殊內外也。 《大雅》云『玄袞赤舄，鉤膺鏤錫』，歌其文也。 《小雅》云『有嚴有翼，共武之服』，詠其武也。 若內外不殊，王制失敘，服妖既作，身隨之亡。 妹嬉冠男子之冠，桀亡天下； 何晏服婦人之服，亦亡其家，其咎均也。」
Director He Yan favored women’s clothing; Fu Xuan said: “This is omen dress. Robes exist to set high against low and inside against outside. The Greater Odes exclaims “black robe, red slippers, hooked breast-straps, chased bells”—praising its ornament. The Lesser Odes cries “solemn, supportive—those martial robes together”—honoring their strength. Blur inner with outer and royal order collapses; garment omens appear—and the wearer perishes. Mo Xi wore a man’s crown—Jie lost the realm; He Yan dressed as a woman—and lost his house; the guilt matches.”
154
吳婦人修容者，急束其發而劘角過於耳，蓋其俗自操束太急，而廉隅失中之謂也。 故吳之風俗，相驅以急，言論彈射，以刻薄相尚。 居三年之喪者，往往有致毀以死。 諸葛患之，著《正交論》，雖不可以經訓整亂，蓋亦救時之作也。
Wu women who styled their looks wrenched their hair tight and cropped temples past the ears—vanity pulled so taut that proportion broke. Hence Wu’s manners chased urgency: words flew like bolts, and cruelty passed for cleverness. Mourners for parents often wasted away unto death. Zhuge Ke fretted and wrote On Proper Associations—not scripture enough to cure chaos, but a tract for its age.
155
孫休後，衣服之制上長下短，又積領五六而裳居一二。 干寶曰：「上饒奢，下儉逼，上有餘下不足之妖也。 」至孫皓，果奢暴恣情於上，而百姓雕困于下，卒以亡國，是其應也。
After Sun Xiu, fashion ran long on top and short below—five or six layered collars against one or two skirt panels. Gan Bao said: “Extravagance reigns aloft while austerity pinches below—a portent of plenty upstairs and want downstairs. ” Under Sun Hao, indulgence and brutality flourished above while commoners were bled dry below; the realm fell—that was the fulfillment.
156
武帝泰始初，衣服上儉下豐，著衣者皆厭䙅，此君衰弱，臣放縱，下掩上之象也。 至元康末，婦人出兩襠，加乎交領之上，此內出外也。 為車乘者苟貴輕細，又數變易其形，皆以白篾為純，蓋古喪車之遺象也。 夫乘者，君子之器。 蓋君子立心無恆，事不崇實也。 干寶以為晉之禍徵也。 及惠帝踐阼，權制在於寵臣，下掩上之應也。 至永嘉末，六宮才人流冗沒于戎狄，內出外之應也。 及天下撓亂，宰輔方伯多負其任，又數改易不崇實之應也。
Early in Emperor Wu’s Taishi era, coats grew tight above and billowing below—every sleeve pooled on the floor: the sovereign enfeebled, his ministers unchecked, the base veiling the crown. Late in Yuankang, women reversed their skirts so the panels rode above the crossed collar—what should stay beneath showed on top. Carriage-makers chased flimsy, ever-changing designs trimmed with white bamboo—echoes of funeral hearses from antiquity. The carriage is the gentleman's proper equipage. It matched gentlemen whose aims shifted and who prized display over substance. Gan Bao read it as a portent of Jin's ruin. When Emperor Hui took the throne, power rested with favored courtiers—the pattern of inferiors overshadowing their sovereign. By Yongjia's end, palace ladies had scattered into barbarian hands—the inner court cast outward among outsiders. As the realm unraveled, ministers and governors failed their posts while titles changed without fixing anything—the omen of empty show.
157
泰始之後，中國相尚用胡床貊槃，及為羌煮貊炙，貴人富室，必畜其器，吉享嘉會，皆以為先。 太康中，又以氈為絈頭及絡帶袴口。 百姓相戲曰，中國必為胡所破。 夫氈毳產于胡，而天下以為絈頭、帶身、袴口，胡既三制之矣，能無敗乎！ 至元康中，氐羌互反，永嘉後，劉、石遂篡中都，自後四夷迭據華土，是服妖之應也。
After Taishi, Central Plains folk embraced alien benches and platters, Qiang-style boiled fare and roasted Mo dishes—the rich stocked them for every banquet. By Taikang, felt wrapped the head, belt, and trouser legs—steppe style on the body. People joked that the heartland would fall to the steppe peoples. Felt comes from the north, yet everyone wrapped head, waist, and ankles in it—the barbarians had claimed three garments off the body; defeat followed. Through Yuankang the Di and Qiang rebelled; after Yongjia Liu and Shi took Luoyang; then outsiders held the heartland—the 'ominous dress' omen fulfilled.
158
初作屐者，婦人頭圓，男子頭方。 圓者順之義，所以別男女也。 至太康初，婦人屐乃頭方，與男無別。 此賈后專妒之徵也。
Early clogs had round toes for women, square for men. Round signified yielding—the line drawn between the sexes. Come Taikang, women's clog toes went square like men's—the distinction blurred. It foretold Empress Jia's jealous grip on power.
159
太康中，天下為《晉世寧》之舞，手接杯盤而反覆之，歌曰「晉世寧，舞杯盤」。 識者曰：「夫樂生人心，所以觀事也。 今接杯盤於手上而反覆之，至危之事也。 杯盤者，酒食之器，而名曰《晉世寧》，言晉世之士苟偷於酒食之間，而知不及遠，晉世之寧猶杯盤之在手也。」
Taikang saw the 'Jin at Peace' dance—hands tossing cups and bowls while singers cried that peace in Jin meant spinning the cups. Critics said music springs from the heart and lays bare the age. Juggling dishes in the hand is peril itself. Cups mean feast and drink, yet the song promises peace—Jin's elite cared only for the banquet; their peace was as fragile as china in the palm.
160
惠帝元康中，婦人之飾有五兵佩，又以金銀玳瑁之屬，為斧鉞戈戟，以當笄。 干寶以為「男女之別，國之大節，故服物異等，贄幣不同。 今婦人而以兵器為飾，此婦人妖之甚者。 於是遂有賈后之事」。 終亡天下。 是時婦人結髮者既成，以繒急束其環，名曰擷子紒。 始自中宮，天下化之。 其後賈后廢害太子之應也。
Yuankang ladies wore jewelry shaped like weapons—metal axes and halberds as hairpins. Gan Bao: gender norms anchor the state—dress and ritual gifts must differ. Arming women with ornaments was prodigy at its worst. Then came Empress Jia's coup against the heir. The dynasty fell. Women finished their coifs, then cinched them tight with silk—the 'plucked-child bun.' The palace set the fashion; the realm copied it. It matched Empress Jia's destruction of the crown prince.
161
元康中，天下始相傚為烏杖以柱掖，其後稍施其鐓，住則植之。 夫木，東方之行，金之臣也。 杖者扶體之器，烏其頭者，尤便用也。 必旁柱掖者，旁救之象也。 施其金，柱則植之，言木因于金，能孤立也。 及懷湣之世，王室多故，而此中都喪敗，元帝以籓臣樹德東方，維持天下，柱掖之應也。 至社稷無主，海內歸之，遂承天命，建都江外，獨立之應也。
Yuankang folk copied crow-head staffs tucked under the arm—later capped with metal ferrules and planted like poles when idle. Wood belongs to the east; it yields to metal. A staff steadies the walker; a crow tip made it handier. Tucking it under the arm suggested sidelong rescue. Metal ferrules let the planted staff stand—wood leaning on metal yet standing alone. When Luoyang fell, Yuan as prince raised the east—exactly the 'underarm brace' sign. When nothing held the center, the realm rallied south—the sign of standing alone became court.
162
元康、太安之間，江淮之域有敗屩自聚於道，多者至四五十量，人或散投坑穀，明日視之復如故。 或云，見狸銜聚之。 干寶以為'夫屩者，人之賤服，處於勞辱，黔庶之象也。 敗者，疲弊之象； 道者，四方往來，所以交通王命也。 今敗屩聚於道者，象黔庶罷病，將相聚為亂，以絕王命也」。 太安中，發壬午兵，百姓怨叛。 江夏張昌唱亂，荊楚從之如流。 於是兵革歲起，服妖也。
Yuankang–Tai'an: tattered sandals heaped on Jiang-Huai roads—scatter them at night, they reappeared by dawn. Some swore foxes stacked them. Gan Bao: sandals are laborers' shoes—the common folk in grime. 'Worn' meant spent strength. Roads carry the king's orders. Sandals heaped on highways meant exhausted masses rising to sever the throne. Tai'an's ren-wu draft drove commoners to revolt. Zhang Chang rose in Jiangxia; Jing-Chu rushed to join him. War followed yearly—the dress omen fulfilled.
163
初，魏造白帢，橫縫其前以別後，名之曰顏帢，傳行之。 至永嘉之間，稍去其縫，名無顏帢，而婦人束發，其緩彌甚，紒之堅不能自立，發被於額，目出而已。 無顏者，愧之言也。 覆額者，慚之貌也。 其緩彌甚者，言天下亡禮與義，放縱情性，及其終極，至於大恥也。 永嘉之後，二帝不反，天下愧焉。
Wei issued white caps with a cross seam front-to-back—the 'face kerchief.' Yongjia dropped the seam—'faceless' caps—and women's buns went slack, hair falling past brows. 'No face' spoke of shame. Hair masking the brow looked like hiding one's face in guilt. The ever-looser binding meant ritual collapsed and appetite ran to utter disgrace. After Yongjia two emperors never came home—the realm hung its head.
164
孝懷帝永嘉中，士大夫競服生箋單衣。 識者指之曰：「此則古者繐衰，諸侯所以服天子也。 今無故服之，殆有應乎！ 」其後遂有胡賊之亂，帝遇害焉。
Yongjia scholars vied to wear stiff raw-paper robes. Critics pointed: that's cui mourning straw—what lords wear for the Son of Heaven. With no bereavement? A bad sign. Then barbarian armies rose and killed the emperor.
165
元帝太興中，兵士以絳囊縛紒。 識者曰：「紒者在首，為乾，君道也。 囊者坤，臣道也。 今以硃囊縛紒，臣道上侵君之象也。 」於是王敦陵上焉。
Daxing troops tied topknots in red silk bags. Critics: the bun crowns the head—Qian, the ruler. The bag is Kun—the minister. Red sack on the ruler's knot—ministers climbing past their lord. Then Wang Dun bullied the throne.
166
舊為羽扇柄者，刻木象其骨形，列羽用十，取全數也。 自中興初，王敦南征，始改為長柄，下出可捉，而減其羽用八。 識者尤之曰：「夫羽扇，翼之名也。 創為長柄者，將執其柄以制羽翼也。 改十為八者，將未備奪已備也。 此殆敦之擅權以制朝廷之柄，又將以無德之材欲竊非據也。 」是時，為衣者又上短，帶才至於掖，著帽者又以帶縛項。 下逼上，上無地也。 為袴者直幅為口，無殺，下大之象。 尋而王敦謀逆，再攻京師。
Old feather fans used ten plumes—the full count. After the court fled south, Wang Dun's campaign brought long handles and cut feathers to eight. Critics: feathers mean wings. A long shaft means seizing the haft to master the wings. Ten cut to eight—strip the prepared of their surplus. It foretold Wang Dun grabbing the reins—unworthy talent eyeing the throne. Meanwhile jackets shrank, belts barely reached the armpit, hat strings choked the neck. Below crowding above—the ruler had nowhere to stand. Trousers went straight-cut and baggy below—the top-heavy omen. Soon Wang Dun rebelled and struck the capital twice.
167
海西嗣位，忘設豹尾。 天戒若曰，夫豹尾，儀服之主，大人所以豹變也。 而海西豹變之日，非所宜忘而忘之。 非主社稷之人，故忘其豹尾，示不終也。 尋而被廢焉。
When Emperor Hai ascended, he omitted the leopard-tail insignia. Heaven warned: the leopard tail crowns ritual dress—the great man's transformation. Yet on the day he should transform, he forgot the very emblem. No true steward of the realm—forgot the tail; doomed not to endure. He was deposed soon after.
168
孝武太元中，人不復著帩頭。 天戒若曰，頭者元首，帩者助元首為儀飾者也。 今忽廢之，若人君獨立無輔佐，以至危亡也。 至安帝，桓玄乃篡位焉。
Taiyuan folk quit wearing forehead cloths. Heaven: the head is supreme; the kerchief aids it as ornament. To shed it was like a ruler bereft of ministers—hurtling toward ruin. Come Emperor An, Huan Xuan seized the throne.
169
舊為屐者，齒皆達楄上，名曰露卯。 太元中忽不徹，名日陰卯。 識者以為卯，謀也，必有陰謀之事。 至烈宗末，驃騎參軍袁悅之始攬構內外，隆安中遂謀詐相傾，以致大亂。
Old clogs had pegs showing above the vamp—'bright mao.' During Taiyuan the waist knots mysteriously would not stay threaded—people nicknamed the garment 'the hidden-mao closure.' Critics: mao puns with 'plot'—conspiracy ahead. Late Liezong, Yuan Yuezhi spun palace intrigue; Long'an brought coups and chaos.
170
太元中，公主婦女必緩鬢傾髻，以為盛飾。 用髲既多，不可恆戴，乃先於木及籠上裝之，名曰假髻，或名假頭。 至於貧家，不能自辦，自號無頭，就人借頭。 遂布天下，亦服妖也。 無幾時，孝武晏駕而天下騷動，刑戮無數，多喪其元。 至於大殮，皆刻木及蠟或縛菰草為頭，是假頭之應云。
Taiyuan noblewomen wore loose side hair and slanted buns as high fashion. Heavy hairpieces could not be worn daily—they mounted them on frames first, 'wig-head.' Poor families called themselves 'headless' and borrowed wigs. The fad spread—a dress omen again. Soon Emperor Xiaowu died; the realm erupted in executions and decapitations. Come burial, families carved wood, wax, or rush heads—the false-head omen fulfilled.
171
桓玄篡立，殿上施絳帳，鏤黃金為顏，四角金龍銜五色羽葆流蘇。 群下相謂曰：「頗類轜車。 」尋而玄敗，此服之妖也。
Huan Xuan's usurpation brought scarlet hall drapes, gold fretwork, dragons at corners trailing colored plumes. Courtiers whispered: looks like a funeral hearse. Huan fell soon after—a costume prodigy.
172
晉末皆冠小而衣裳博大，風流相放，輿臺成俗。 識者曰：「上小而下大，此禪代之象也。 」尋而宋受終焉。
Late Jin: tiny caps, billowing robes—fashion aped even by servants. Critics: small top, big bottom—the abdication sign. Song took the mandate soon after.
173
=
Typographical section divider before the subsection on fowl prodigies.
174
雞禍
Chicken Omens
175
=魏明帝，廷尉府中雌雞化為雄，不鳴不將。 干寶曰：「是歲宣帝平遼東，百姓始有與能之義，此其象也。 然晉三后並以人臣終，不鳴不將，又天意也。」
Wei Mingdi: in the Court of Justice yard a hen became a rooster—it did not crow and did not lead the flock. Gan Bao: that year the court pacified Liaodong and the people learned to yield to the worthy—that matched one half of the sign; yet three Jin empresses all ended as mere subjects—still silent, still not leading: Heaven's intent again.
176
惠帝，陳國有雞生雄雞無翅，既大，墜坑而死。 王隱以為：「雄者，胤嗣子之象。 坑者，母象。 今雞生無翅，墜坑而死，此子無羽翼，為母所陷害乎？ 」于後賈后誣殺湣懷，此其應也。
Under Emperor Hui, Chen reported a hen that hatched a wingless cockerel; when it had grown, it tumbled into a pit and died. Wang Yin read the sign: "The male stands for heirs—the succession. The pit stands for the mother. The chick hatched flightless and died in the pit—did it mean the prince had no shelter and would be undone by the mother figure? " Later Empress Jia framed and murdered Crown Prince Min Huai—the omen had spoken.
177
太安中，周玘家雌雞逃承溜中，六七日而下，奮翼鳴將，獨毛羽不變。 其後有陳敏之事。 敏雖控制江表，終無紀綱文章，殆其象也。 卒為玘所滅。 雞禍見玘家，又天意也。 京房《易傳》曰：「牝雞雄鳴，主不榮。」
During Tai'an a hen at Zhou Qi's house hid in the gutter; a week later she emerged, beat her wings and crowed like a cock, yet her plumage stayed hen. Then came Chen Min's rebellion. Chen Min held the southeast but never built lasting rule—that may have been the point of the sign. Zhou Qi destroyed him in the end. The omen chose Zhou Qi's roof—Heaven marking its meaning again. Jing Fang's Yi zhuan warns: "A hen that crows like a cock means the ruler will not endure."
178
元帝太興中，王敦鎮武昌，有雌雞化為雄。 天戒若曰，雌化為雄，臣陵其上。 其後王敦再攻京師。
Under Emperor Yuan, during Taixing, while Wang Dun held Wuchang, a hen turned into a rooster. The celestial warning read: female turning male—subjects lording it over the throne. Wang Dun then struck the capital twice.
179
孝武四月，廣陵高平閻嵩家雌雞生無右翅，彭城人劉象之家雞有三足。 京房《易傳》曰：「君用婦人言，則雞生妖。 」是時，主相並用尼媼之言，寵賜過厚，故妖象見焉。
In the fourth month of Emperor Xiaowu's reign, Yan Song of Gaoping in Guangling had a hen hatch a chick without its right wing, and Liu Xiang of Pengcheng owned a three-legged fowl. Jing Fang's Yi zhuan says: "When the sovereign listens to women's counsel, fowl breed freaks. " Throne and regent alike heeded nursemaids and old wives; patronage ran extravagant—so the creature showed its warning.
180
安帝八月，琅邪王道子家青雌雞化為赤雄雞，不鳴不將。 桓玄將篡，不能成業之象。
In Emperor An's eighth month, at Prince Sima Daozi's mansion a blue hen became a scarlet cock—it neither crowed nor ruled the yard. An emblem of Huan Xuan seizing power without finishing what he started.
181
四年，荊州有雞生角，角尋墮落。 是時桓玄始擅西夏，狂慢不肅，故有雞禍。 天戒若曰，角，兵象，尋墮落者，暫起不終之妖也。 後皆應也。
In the fourth year a Jingzhou fowl sprouted horns; they dropped away almost at once. Huan Xuan had seized the upper Yangzi and strutted without discipline—the fowl omen matched his temper. Heaven hinted: horns mean war; when they fell quickly, the rise would be brief. Every detail later came true.
182
，衡陽有雌雞化為雄，八十日而冠萎。 天戒若曰，衡陽，桓玄楚國之邦略也。 及桓玄篡位，果八十日而敗，此其應也。
That same year in Hengyang a hen turned cock; on the eightieth day its comb shriveled. The warning fixed on Hengyang—heartland of Huan Xuan's would-be Chu. When Huan Xuan took the throne, he fell exactly eighty days later—the reckoning held.
183
=
Typographical section divider.
184
青祥
Green Omens
185
=武帝八月丁酉，大風折大社樹，有青氣出焉，此青祥也。 占曰：「東莞當有帝者。 」明年，元帝生。 是時，帝大父武王封東莞，由是徙封琅邪。 孫盛以為中興之表。 晉室之亂，武帝子孫無孑遺，社樹折之應，又常風之罰。
Tradition relates: on the dingyou day of the eighth month of Emperor Wu of Jin, a gale snapped the great soil-altar tree and green mists rose—the green omen. The oracle read: "A ruler will rise from Dongguan. " The next year Emperor Yuan was born. His great-grandfather the Prince of Wu had held Dongguan before the house moved its fief to Langye. Sun Sheng read it as a marker of the dynasty's return. The wars erased Sima Yan's line—the sacred tree's fall and the restless winds were Heaven's sentence.
186
惠帝元康中，洛陽南山有虻作聲，曰「韓屍屍」。 識者曰：「韓氏將屍也，言屍屍者，盡死意也。 」其後韓謐誅而韓族殲焉，此青祥也。
Under Emperor Hui in the Yuan-kang years, horseflies on Luoyang's southern hills seemed to buzz "Han corpses, corpses." Those who knew prognostication said: "The Han surname line is headed for corpses—the doubled shi means total extinction. " Han Mi died and his kin were rooted out—another green omen fulfilled.
187
=
Typographical section divider.
188
金沴木
Metal Harms Wood
189
=魏文帝正月，幸許昌。 許昌城南門無故自崩，帝心惡之，遂不入，還洛陽。 此金沴木，木動之也。 五月，宮車晏駕。 京房《易傳》曰：「上下咸悖，厥妖也城門壞。」
Tradition relates: in the first month Cao Pi, Emperor Wen of Wei, traveled to Xuchang. Xuchang's south gate suddenly buckled; uneasy, the emperor turned back to Luoyang without entering. Metal overwhelming Wood—the timbers had buckled. That fifth month the emperor died. Jing Fang: "When high and low turn against each other, gates crumble as the portent."
190
元帝六月，吳郡米廡無故自壞。 天戒若曰，夫米廡，貨糴之屋，無故自壞，此五穀踴貴，所以無糴賣也。 是歲遂大饑，死者千數焉。
In Emperor Yuan's sixth month Wu commandery's rice warehouse suddenly collapsed. Heaven warned: a granary supplies grain—when it falls on its own, prices spike and trade stops. Famine followed; thousands perished.
191
明帝太甯元年，周莚自歸王敦，既立其宅宇，所起五間六梁，一時躍出墜地，餘桁猶亙柱頭。 此金沴木也。 明年五月，錢鳳謀亂，遂族滅莚，而湖熟尋亦為墟矣。
In Ming Emperor's Tai'ning 1, Zhou Yan—fresh from joining Wang Dun—watched the five-by-six frame of his new hall leap from its footings; loose purlins alone still bridged the posts. Textbook Metal-harms-Wood lore. The next May Qian Feng rebelled; Zhou Yan's house was wiped out and Hushu soon lay waste.
192
安帝正月丙子，會稽王世子元顯將討桓玄，建牙竿于揚州南門，其東者難立，良久乃正。 近沴妖也。 而元顯尋為玄所擒。
On bingzi in Emperor An's first month, Sima Yuanxian prepared to strike Huan Xuan and planted his banner pole at Yangzhou's south gate—the eastern mast long refused to stand straight. A related species of baleful sign. Yuanxian soon fell into Huan Xuan's hands.
193
三年五月，樂賢堂壞。 時帝嚚眊，無樂賢之心，故此堂是沴。
In the third year's fifth month the Hall for Delighting in Worthies fell. The sovereign was deaf to counsel and cared nothing for worthies—the hall mirrored him.
194
五月，國子聖堂壞。 天戒若曰，聖堂，禮樂之本，無故自壞，業祚將墜之象。 未及十年而禪位焉。
That May the National University's ritual hall caved in. Heaven warned: the ritual hall anchors ceremony—its ruin foretold the throne slipping away. Within a decade he had abdicated.
